concepts.name: Awareness
concepts.definition: perception or knowledge of something. Accurate reportability of something perceived or known is widely used as a behavioral index of conscious awareness. However, it is possible to be aware of something without being explicitly conscious of it (e.g., see blindsight)

concepts.name: north-south orientation
concepts.definition: assessment of the north-south cardinal orientation

concepts.name: Reactive Control
concepts.definition: During reactive mode, cognitive control is transiently activated only after the cognitively demanding event has occurred.

concepts.name: anxiety sensitivity
concepts.definition: Anxiety Sensitivity (AS) is defined in terms of fear of anxiety-related sensations due to beliefs about what those sensations mean (Reiss et al., 1986)

concepts.name: Venturesomeness
concepts.definition: Venturesomeness is defined as being conscious of the risk but acting anyway.

concepts.name: Interpersonal Conflict
concepts.definition: disagreement or discord between people with respect to goals, values, or attitudes.

concepts.name: abductive reasoning
concepts.definition: The process of adopting an explanatory hypothesis; inferring the cause A as a possible explanation for the consequence B.

concepts.name: abstract analogy
concepts.definition: high-level analogy that retains general information relevant to many specific instances

concepts.name: abstract knowledge
concepts.definition: Knowledge that is general and not tied to a specific instance.

concepts.name: acoustic coding
concepts.definition: a type of short term memory coding that represents the acoustic properties of the signal

concepts.name: acoustic encoding
concepts.definition: the processing and encoding of auditory input for storage and later retrieval.

concepts.name: acoustic phonetic processing
concepts.definition: the cognitive ability to discriminate items on the basis of contrasts in sonorance, manner, place, or voicing in auditory stimuli.

concepts.name: acoustic processing
concepts.definition: the extraction of information from signals propagated undersea, in the atmosphere, or in the solid earth in the presence of acoustic noise.

concepts.name: action
concepts.definition: the bringing about of an alteration by force or through a natural agency; expression by means of attitude, voice, and gesture; a function of the body or one of its parts; an act of will; a thing done; the accomplishment of a thing usually over a period of time, in stages, or with the possibility of repetition.

concepts.name: activation
concepts.definition: the relative engagement of a particular mental representation compared to other representations

concepts.name: activation level
concepts.definition: quantity or amount of activation

concepts.name: adaptation
concepts.definition: adjustment to environmental conditions; adjustment of a sense organ to the intensity or quality of stimulation; modification of an organism or its parts that makes it more fit for existence under the conditions of its environment.

concepts.name: adaptive control
concepts.definition: modifying the control law used by a controller to cope with the fact that the parameters of the system being controlled are slowly time-varying or uncertain.

concepts.name: affect perception
concepts.definition: The ability to understand a facial, vocal, or gestural behavior that serves as an indicator of emotion.

concepts.name: affect recognition
concepts.definition: The ability to understand a physical expression that serves as an indicator of emotion.

concepts.name: altruism
concepts.definition: helping others in the absence of an immediately obvious reward.

concepts.name: altruistic motivation
concepts.definition: A desire or need to help others driven by selflessness.

concepts.name: alveolar
concepts.definition: speech sound articulated with the tip of the tongue touching or near the teethridge.

concepts.name: amodal representation
concepts.definition: The way the brain codes multiple inputs such as words and pictures to integrate and create a larger conceptual idea; independent of a particular modality

concepts.name: analog representation
concepts.definition: a value or variable in analog form.

concepts.name: analogical encoding
concepts.definition: the structural comparison of a familiar with a novel situation

concepts.name: analogical inference
concepts.definition: is the ability to reason by permitting the extension of knowledge of a target domain by virtue of its similarity to a base domain. The general procedure for analogical inference involves copying structure from the base to the target in which missing information is generated, and substitutions are made for items for which analogical correspondences have already been found.

concepts.name: analogical problem solving
concepts.definition: using principles or concepts from a well-understood situation to solve problems in a new domain or area

concepts.name: analogical reasoning
concepts.definition: a method of processing information that compares the similarities between new and understood concepts, then uses those similarities to gain understanding of the new concept; a form of inductive reasoning.

concepts.name: analogical transfer
concepts.definition: The transfer of knowledge from one situation to another by finding a set of one-to-one correspondences between aspects of one body of information and aspects of another.

concepts.name: analogy
concepts.definition: inference that if two or more things agree with one another in some respects they will probably agree in others; resemblance in some particulars between things otherwise unlike; correspondence between the members of pairs or sets of linguistic forms that serves as a basis for the creation of another form; correspondence in function between anatomical parts of different structure and origin.

concepts.name: anchoring
concepts.definition: a cognitive bias that describes the common human tendency to rely too heavily, or "anchor," on one trait or piece of information when making decisions.

concepts.name: anticipation
concepts.alias: intuition, foreknowledge, prescience, foresight, prediction, imaginative speculation
concepts.definition: prior expectation of an event or occurrence, sometimes accompanied by an emotional reaction

concepts.name: apparent motion
concepts.definition: The illusory perception that movement is occurring in one or more static images.

concepts.name: apperception
concepts.definition: the process by which new experience is assimilated to and transformed by the residuum of past experience of an individual to form a new whole.

concepts.name: appetitive motivation
concepts.definition: behavior directed toward goals that are usually associated with positive hedonic processes.

concepts.name: arousal
concepts.definition: Disambiguation

concepts.name: articulation
concepts.definition: the act of vocally producing an utterance or expression

concepts.name: articulatory planning
concepts.definition: The action of coordinating complex tongue and mouth movements in order to produce sound.

concepts.name: articulatory rehearsal
concepts.definition: the process of subvocally repeating material that is to be stored in memory.

concepts.name: assimilation
concepts.definition: the process of receiving new facts or of responding to new situations in conformity with what is already available to consciousness.

concepts.name: association
concepts.definition: the process of forming mental connections or bonds between sensations, ideas, or memories.

concepts.name: association learning
concepts.definition: learning process in which two or more items or concepts become associated with each other; often used in relation to learned stimulus-response associations

concepts.name: attachment
concepts.definition: a social connection between individuals

concepts.name: attended channel
concepts.definition: the particular input, out of two or more, that is consciously perceived due to attention.

concepts.name: attended stimulus
concepts.definition: the specific object in the environment on which attention is focused.

concepts.name: attention
concepts.definition: used to describe any number of cognitive processes, organized as top-down or bottom-up, goal-directed or stimulus-driven, and more, but generally reflecting an interplay between cognitive and sensory systems.

concepts.name: attention capacity
concepts.definition: refers to the extent that one can allocate their processing resources.

concepts.name: attentional effort
concepts.definition: a motivated activation of attention systems in order to stabilize or recover attentional performance in response to the detection of errors and reward loss or, more generally, deteriorating attentional performance; amount of attentional resources needed for a particular situation; engagement of attentional resources

concepts.name: attentional resources
concepts.definition: amount of available attentional capacity

concepts.name: attentional state
concepts.definition: referring to amount of attentional resources being engaged;  a relaxed attentional state requires little attentional effort, whereas an alert, focused attentional state requires more

concepts.name: attitude
concepts.definition: a mental position with regard to a fact or state

concepts.name: audiovisual perception
concepts.definition: a single unified awareness derived from the integration of auditory and visual sensory processes when a audiovisual stimulus is present.

concepts.name: audition
concepts.definition: the sense or act of hearing.

concepts.name: auditory attention
concepts.definition: is the cognitive process of selectively concentrating on one auditory stream in the environment while ignoring others.

concepts.name: auditory coding
concepts.definition: processing and encoding of sound, words, and all other auditory input for storage and later retrieval. According to Baddeley, processing of auditory information is aided by the concept of the phonological loop, which allows input within our echoic memory.

concepts.name: auditory encoding
concepts.definition: the process of storing auditory information in memory.

concepts.name: auditory feedback
concepts.definition: is provided by auditory stimulation in response to specific behavior. The feedback may be used to amend subsequent behavior, cognition, perception or performance.

concepts.name: auditory grouping
concepts.definition: joining disparate sounds together into one percept; assessing which acoustic streams belong together

concepts.name: auditory imagery
concepts.definition: the subjective experience of hearing in the absence of auditory stimulation.

concepts.name: auditory learning
concepts.definition: learning of auditorily presented information

concepts.name: auditory lexical access
concepts.definition: The process by which the basic sound-meaning connections of language, i.e., lexical entries, are activated.

concepts.name: auditory localization
concepts.definition: a listener's ability to identify the location or origin of a detected sound.

concepts.name: auditory masking
concepts.definition: the perception of one sound is affected by the presence of another sound; presenting a sound to interfere with or terminate a target sound

concepts.name: auditory memory
concepts.definition: the cognitive capacity of storing and retrieving information related to sound.

concepts.name: auditory perception
concepts.definition: The ability to identify, interpret, and attach meaning to sound.

concepts.name: auditory scene
concepts.definition: auditory scene analysis is the process by which the human auditory system organizes sound into perceptually meaningful elements.

concepts.name: auditory scene analysis
concepts.definition: the process by which the human auditory system organizes sound into perceptually meaningful elements.

concepts.name: auditory sentence comprehension
concepts.definition: ability to combine auditory words into a meaningful sentence unit.

concepts.name: auditory stream segregation
concepts.definition: the perceptual grouping of sounds to form coherent representations of objects in the acoustic scene; a fundamental aspect of hearing and speech perception.

concepts.name: auditory word comprehension
concepts.definition: ability to parse acoustic signals into meaningful words

concepts.name: auditory word recognition
concepts.definition: ability to recognize acoustically presented words

concepts.name: auditory working memory
concepts.definition: Working memory for auditory information

concepts.name: autobiographical memory
concepts.definition: a memory system consisting of episodes recollected from an individualâs life, based on a combination of episodic (personal experiences and specific objects, people and events experienced at particular time and place) and semantic (general knowledge and facts about the world) memory.

concepts.name: autobiographical recall
concepts.definition: episodes recollected from an individualâs life, based on a combination of episodic (personal experiences and specific objects, people and events experienced at particular time and place) and semantic (general knowledge and facts about the world) memory.

concepts.name: automaticity
concepts.definition: behavior performed without intention

concepts.name: availability heuristic
concepts.definition: A heuristic in which people predict the frequency of classes or the probability of events based on the ease with which relevant instances come to mind.

concepts.name: aversive learning
concepts.definition: behavior modification using an adverse stimulus in response to the inappropriate or undesirable behavior.

concepts.name: backward chaining
concepts.definition: an inference method used in automated theorem provers, proof assistants and other artificial intelligence applications.  Backward chaining starts with a list of goals (or a hypothesis) and works backwards from the consequent to the antecedent to see if there is data available that will support any of these consequents.

concepts.name: behavioral inhibition
concepts.definition: Disambiguation

concepts.name: belief
concepts.definition: a state or habit of mind in which trust or confidence is placed in some person or thing; conviction of the truth of some statement or the reality of some being or phenomenon especially when based on examination of evidence.

concepts.name: binocular convergence
concepts.definition: when you look at an object that is closer than approximately 25 feet, your eyes must converge on the object to perceive it as a single object clearly in focus."

concepts.name: binocular disparity
concepts.definition: the difference in image location of an object seen by the left and right eyes, resulting from the eyes' horizontal separation. The brain uses binocular disparity to extract depth information from the two-dimensional retinal images  in stereopsis.

concepts.name: binocular vision
concepts.definition: is vision in which both eyes are used together.  Having two eyes confers at least four advantages over having one. First, it gives a creature a spare eye in case one is damaged. Second, it gives a wider field of view.  Third, it gives binocular summation in which the ability to detect faint objects is enhanced.  Fourth it can give stereopsis in which parallax provided by the two eyes' different positions on the head give precise depth perception.  Such binocular vision is usually accompanied by singleness of vision or binocular fusion, in which a single image is seen despite each eye's having its own image of any object.  Other phenomena of binocular vision include utrocular discrimination, eye dominance, allelotropia, and binocular rivalry.

concepts.name: bitterness
concepts.definition: being or inducing the one of the four basic taste sensations that is peculiarly acrid, astringent, or disagreeable; marked by intensity or severity; marked by cynicism and rancor; intensely unpleasant especially in coldness or rawness; expressive of severe pain, grief, or regret.

concepts.name: body orientation
concepts.definition: perception of the orientation of the body overall relative to other objects in the environment

concepts.name: capacity limitation
concepts.definition: a limitation on the capacity to process information

concepts.name: case based reasoning
concepts.definition: the process of solving new problems based on the solutions of similar past problems.

concepts.name: categorical clustering
concepts.definition: the clustering of recalled items based on category membership

concepts.name: categorical knowledge
concepts.definition: knowledge about different attributes and uses of an object that allows it to be placed in a group of objects with similar attributes and uses.

concepts.name: categorical perception
concepts.definition: A form of perception in which the individual perceives a categorical distinction rather than a continuous scale of a varying perceptual feature.

concepts.name: categorization
concepts.definition: The assignment of a stimulus to one of a set of categories

concepts.name: category based induction
concepts.definition: requires that information about one set of categories is used to infer something about another category. A set of premises establishes that one or more categories possess a certain property.  The premises are followed by an assertion (the conclusion) that a target category also possesses that property.

concepts.name: category learning
concepts.definition: is a strategy which requires a learner to compare and contrast groups or categories that contain concept-relevant features with groups or categories that do not contain concept-relevant features.

concepts.name: causal inference
concepts.definition: The process of inferring that one state/object/event causes the occurrence of another state/object/event.

concepts.name: central attention
concepts.definition: is the cognitive process that allows one to focus on the most important and relevant train of thought that needs to be attended to in a specific situation.

concepts.name: centration
concepts.definition: the tendency to focus on one aspect of a situation and neglect others.

concepts.name: chemonociception
concepts.definition: perception of stimulation by noxious chemical agents

concepts.name: chromatic contrast
concepts.definition: When a small patch is surrounded by a color field, the patch appears to be tinted in the opponent color of the surrounding field.

concepts.name: chunk
concepts.definition: Structure in memory that is used as a unit of knowledge representation. Also refers to the process of learning by which these units are acquired.

concepts.name: chunking
concepts.definition:
The process of recoding information by splitting or reorganizing it into smaller parts. 
Actually: combining several smaller items into a larger "group" item, i.e.: 3 separate "incoming aircraft" considered as "3 incoming aircraft". Significantly reduces the working memory space used. Likely concept model for computer programming data-forms that list pointers to numerous specific data. Larger classes of concepts include: Learning and Memory, Attention, Action (Planning), Executive Control.

concepts.name: cognitive development
concepts.definition: the construction of thought processes, including remembering, problem solving, and decision-making, from childhood through adolescence to adulthood.

concepts.name: cognitive dissonance
concepts.definition: The mental state in which a person holds multiple conflicting ideas simultaneously

concepts.name: cognitive effort
concepts.definition: Consciously or intentionally engaging cognitive resources in order to achieve a particular end.

concepts.name: cognitive heuristic
concepts.definition: are simple, efficient rules, hard-coded by evolutionary processes or learned, which have been proposed to explain how people make decisions, come to judgments, and solve problems, typically when facing complex problems or incomplete information. These rules work well under most circumstances, but in certain cases lead to systematic errors or cognitive biases.

concepts.name: cognitive load
concepts.definition: The amount of demand placed on working memory, typically expressed along some continuum and within a theoretical maximum.

concepts.name: cognitive map
concepts.definition: a type of mental processing composed of a series of psychological transformations by which an individual can acquire, code, store, recall, and decode information about the relative locations and attributes of phenomena in their everyday or metaphorical spatial environment.

concepts.name: color perception
concepts.definition: The process of distinguishing objects based on the wavelengths of the light they reflect or emit.

concepts.name: communication
concepts.definition: a process by which information is exchanged between individuals through a common system of symbols, signs, or behavior.

concepts.name: competition
concepts.definition: the act or process of competing; active demand by two or more organisms or kinds of organisms for some environmental resource in short supply; a contest between rivals.

concepts.name: concept
concepts.definition: a cognitive unit of meaningâan abstract  idea or a mental symbol  sometimes defined as a "unit of knowledge," built from other units which act as a concept's characteristics.

concepts.name: concept learning
concepts.definition: Concept learning, also known as category learning and concept attainment, is largely based on the works of the cognitive psychologist Jerome Bruner. Bruner, Goodnow, & Austin (1967) defined concept attainment (or concept learning) as "the search for and listing of attributes that can be used to distinguish exemplars from non exemplars of various categories." More simply put, concepts are the mental categories that help us classify objects, events, or ideas and each object, event, or idea has a set of common relevant features. Thus, concept learning is a strategy which requires a learner to compare and contrast groups or categories that contain concept-relevant features with groups or categories that do not contain concept-relevant features.

concepts.name: conceptual category
concepts.definition: a way of organizing information, generally derived from experience; they can be part of a hierarchy, as in a taxonomy, or without, as in an alphabet.

concepts.name: conceptual coherence
concepts.definition: combining a set concepts to make sense of a situation or set of situations.

concepts.name: conceptual planning
concepts.definition: in linguistics, a flexible process of preparation pertaining to grammatical structure of clauses, occurring both before and during production thereof

concepts.name: conceptual skill
concepts.definition: is the ability to form concepts about abstract and complex ideas such as communication, language, time, and money, for example.

concepts.name: conceptualization
concepts.definition: to form a concept of; to interpret.

concepts.name: conditional reasoning
concepts.definition: the reasoner must draw a conclusion based on a conditional, or âifâ¦then,â proposition.

concepts.name: conflict detection
concepts.definition: arises in the presence of concurrently active, mutually exclusive representations

concepts.name: conjunction search
concepts.definition: the process of searching for a target that is not defined by any single unique visual feature, but by a combination of two or more features.

concepts.name: connotation
concepts.definition: the suggesting of a meaning by a word apart from the thing it explicitly names or describes; something suggested by a word or thing; the signification of something; an essential property or group of properties of a thing named by a term in logic.

concepts.name: consciousness
concepts.definition: the quality or state of being aware especially of something within oneself; the state or fact of being conscious of an external object, state, or fact; the state of being characterized by sensation, emotion, volition, and thought; the totality of conscious states of an individual; the normal state of conscious life,(regained consciousness); the upper level of mental life of which the person is aware as contrasted with unconscious processes.

concepts.name: constancy
concepts.definition: steadfastness of mind under duress; a state of being constant or unchanging.

concepts.name: constituent structure
concepts.definition: is an analysis, often in the form of a schematic representation, of the constituents of a construction, such as a sentence.

concepts.name: context
concepts.definition: A set of interrelated conditions in which something exists or occurs (e.g., a style of language in a particular passage, activity of a given regions given sensory input).

concepts.name: context dependent
concepts.definition: is a class of memory that refers to improved recall of specific episodes or information when the context present at encoding and retrieval are the same.

concepts.name: context memory
concepts.definition: refers to improved recall of specific episodes or information when the context present at encoding and retrieval are similar.

concepts.name: contextual knowledge
concepts.definition: information, and/or skills that have particular meaning because of the conditions that form part of their description.

concepts.name: contingency learning
concepts.definition: Learning of the contingencies between different events

concepts.name: contrastive stress
concepts.definition: No definition submitted yet

concepts.name: conventionality
concepts.definition: the quality, fact, or condition of being conventional; conventional behavior or act; a conventional form, usage, or rule.

concepts.name: convergent thinking
concepts.definition: analytical, usually deductive, thinking in which ideas are examined for their logical validity or in which a set of rules is followed.

concepts.name: conversation
concepts.definition: An exchange of sentiments, observations, opinions, or ideas.

concepts.name: conversational skill
concepts.definition: Ability to engage in appropriate communication of sentiments, observations, opinions, or ideas through dialogue.

concepts.name: conversational speech
concepts.definition: is interactive, more-or-less spontaneous, communication between two or more conversants. Interactivity occurs because contributions to a conversation are response reactions to what has previously been said. Spontaneity occurs because a conversation must proceed, to some extent, and in some way, unpredictably.

concepts.name: conversational structure
concepts.definition: is the organization of interactive, more-or-less spontaneous, communication between two or more conversants.

concepts.name: coordination
concepts.definition: is the act of coordinating, making different people or things work together for a goal or effect.

concepts.name: coproduction
concepts.definition: No definition submitted yet

concepts.name: coreference
concepts.definition: a relationship between two words or phrases in which both refer to the same person or thing and one stands as a linguistic antecedent of the other.

concepts.name: creative cognition
creative problem solving
concepts.definition: the mental process of independently creating a solution to a problem without learned assistance.

concepts.name: creative thinking
concepts.definition: the intellectually disciplined process of actively and skillfully conceptualizing, applying, analyzing, synthesizing, and/or evaluating information gathered from, or generated by, observation, experience, reflection, reasoning, or communication, as a guide to belief and action (Scriven & Paul, 1992).

concepts.name: critical period
concepts.definition: a limited time in which an event can occur, usually to result in some kind of transformation; in developmental psychology and developmental biology, it is a time in the early stages of an organism's life during which it displays a heightened sensitivity to certain environmental stimuli, and develops in particular ways due to experiences at this time.

concepts.name: crosstalk
concepts.definition: interference by information presented via multiple channels

concepts.name: crystallized intelligence
concepts.definition: the ability to utilize previously acquired knowledge and experience.

concepts.name: cue dependent forgetting
concepts.definition: is the failure to recall a memory due to missing stimuli or cues that were present at the time the memory was encoded.

concepts.name: cue validity
concepts.definition: the conditional probability that an object falls in a particular category given a particular feature or cue.

concepts.name: cueing
concepts.definition: to give/present a stimulus that prompts a reaction.

concepts.name: dative shift
concepts.definition: a grammatical process by which an oblique  argument of a verb, usually one functioning as a recipient or a benefactive (roles often expressed by datives), is placed in the same grammatical role as a patient, increasing the valency of the verb and forming a clause with two objects.

concepts.name: decay of activation
concepts.definition: An explanation for why spreading activation, in network-based models of knowledge representation, peters out as a function of the distance between nodes.

concepts.name: deception
concepts.definition: an act to propagate beliefs that are not true, or not the whole truth (as in half-truths or omission).

concepts.name: decision making
concepts.definition: The deliberate selection of a single alternative amongst multiple alternatives.

concepts.name: declarative knowledge
concepts.definition: Knowledge that is descriptive and includes knowing "that" rather than knowing "how" (can be expressed in declarative sentences).

concepts.name: declarative memory
concepts.definition: Memory for facts, and that can be intentionally articulated in some manner.

concepts.name: declarative rule
concepts.definition: A criterion for which one possesses declarative knowledge. Contrasts with an implicit or non-declarative rule, which one might follow but not represent as a rule or even be aware that they are following.

concepts.name: deductive inference
concepts.definition: A type of inference in which the conclusion always follows from the stated premises.If the premises are true, then the conclusion is valid.

concepts.name: deductive reasoning
concepts.definition: is reasoning which constructs or evaluates deductive arguments. Deductive arguments are attempts to show that a conclusion necessarily follows from a set of premises or hypotheses.

concepts.name: deep processing
concepts.definition: Evaluating a piece of information in terms of meaning or associations to other concepts as opposed to surface or incidental characteristics.

concepts.name: deep structure
concepts.definition: The essential meaning of a sentence, without regard to the grammatical features (surface structure) of the sentence that are needed to express it in words.

concepts.name: depth cue
concepts.definition: Depth perception arises from a variety of depth cues. These are typically classified into binocular cues that require input from both eyes and monocular cues that require the input from just one eye.  Binocular cues include stereopsis, yielding depth from binocular vision through exploitation of parallax. Monocular cues include size: distant objects subtend smaller visual angles than near objects.  A third class of cues requires synthetic integration of binocular and monocular cues.

concepts.name: depth perception
concepts.definition: Ability to perceive the visual world in three dimensions.

concepts.name: desire
concepts.definition: to long or hope for, exhibit or feel desire for; to express a wish for.

concepts.name: diphthong
concepts.definition: a gliding monosyllabic speech sound (as the vowel combination at the end of toy) that starts at or near the articulatory position for one vowel and moves to or toward the position of another.

concepts.name: dispositions
concepts.definition: Tendency to act in a particular manner given a certain set of antecedents.

concepts.name: distraction
concepts.definition: Any event that interrupts a mental process.

concepts.name: distributed coding
concepts.definition: A type of coding in which the information that constitutes a concept (or mental representation) is spread amongst a number of constituent representations.

concepts.name: divergent thinking
concepts.definition: a thought process or method used to generate creative ideas by exploring many possible solutions.

concepts.name: divided attention
concepts.definition: A state in which the focus of attention is spread across more than one object or event.

concepts.name: dream
concepts.definition: a succession of thoughts, images, sounds or emotions which the mind experiences during sleep.

concepts.name: efficiency
concepts.definition: effective operation as measured by a comparison of production with cost (as in energy, time, money, or cortical activity)

concepts.name: effort
concepts.definition: Consciously or intentionally engaging resources in order to achieve a particular end.

concepts.name: effortful processing
concepts.definition: learning or storing (encoding) that requires attention and effort.

concepts.name: egocentric
concepts.definition: A frame of reference centered around the self. In perception, a first-person frame of reference.

concepts.name: elaborative processing
concepts.definition: Processing in which semantic associations or relations between words/concepts are generated or elaborated on.

concepts.name: emotion
concepts.definition: a complex of psychological phenomena that involve some degree of arousal and valence (positive/negative)

concepts.name: emotional decision making
concepts.definition: The use of affective information as information in a decision making process or as a basis for making a decision. Hot cognition.

concepts.name: emotional expression
concepts.definition: observable verbal and nonverbal behavior that communicates emotion with or without self-awareness.

concepts.name: emotional intelligence
concepts.definition: the capacity, skill or ability to identify, assess, and manage the emotions of one's self, of others, and of groups.

concepts.name: emotional memory
concepts.definition: Emotional memory is the storage and recall of events and details that are couple with the physiological response that was present when the event occurred.

concepts.name: emotional mimicry
concepts.definition: is the ability of a person to imitate, copy, and experience the physical and emotional characteristics of another persons emotion.

concepts.name: emotional suppression
concepts.definition: A process to reduce or inhibit the impact of an emotion on ones current conscious state or behavior.

concepts.name: episodic learning
concepts.definition: a change in behavior that occurs as a result of an event; episodic learning is so named because events are recorded into episodic memory.

concepts.name: episodic memory
concepts.definition: memory of autobiographical events (times, places, associated emotions, and other contextual knowledge) that can be explicitly stated.

concepts.name: error detection
concepts.definition: Processes that identify when an error has been made.

concepts.name: error signal
concepts.definition: An event following error detection, in which a sign is relayed notifying the advent of an error.

concepts.name: error trapping
concepts.definition: procedures that detect and correct errors before the errors cause further confusion.

concepts.name: excitation
concepts.definition: a state of increased emotional arousal

concepts.name: expertise
concepts.definition: Having a highly cultivated level of skill in a particular domain. Occurs after prolonged experience in a domain.

concepts.name: explicit knowledge
concepts.definition: Knowledge that can be articulated or expressed intentionally.

concepts.name: explicit learning
concepts.definition: Acquisition of skills and/or knowledge actively and with awareness. Typically such learning is accompanied by meta-awareness - individuals can explain how they acquired the skill/knowledge.

concepts.name: explicit memory
concepts.definition: the conscious, intentional recollection of previous experiences and information.

concepts.name: extrinsic motivation
concepts.definition: motivated by external factors, as opposed to the internal drivers of intrinsic motivation. Extrinsic motivation drives one to do things for tangible rewards or pressures.

concepts.name: face perception
concepts.definition: The processes by which faces are identified as such.

concepts.name: face recognition
concepts.definition: The process of determining whether a face is the same as another face that has been previously encountered.

concepts.name: facial expression
concepts.definition: Movements and positions of the facial muscles that can be used as a form of nonverbal communication, particularly in conveying emotional states.

concepts.name: false memory
concepts.definition: a memory that refers to an event that did not actually occur

concepts.name: feature extraction
concepts.definition: Processes by which relevant aspects of a data stream are separated from irrelevant aspects.

concepts.name: feedback processing
concepts.definition: Evaluative or corrective information about an action, event, or process delivered to the original or controlling source, often with the intent of modifying future actions.

concepts.name: filtering
concepts.definition: a device or process that removes from a signal some unwanted component or feature.

concepts.name: fixation
concepts.definition: Maintaining gaze or attention on some object or event. (Experimental design) A trial period in which a participant is instructed to direct attention toward a visual stimulus (often a cross).

concepts.name: fixed action patterns
concepts.definition: an instinctive  behavioral  sequence that is indivisible and runs to completion.

concepts.name: fluid intelligence
concepts.definition: a factor of general intelligence originally identified by Raymond Cattell; Cattell defined fluid intelligence as "â¦the ability to perceive relationships independent of previous specific practice or instruction concerning those relationships." Fluid intelligence is the ability to think and reason abstractly and solve problems. This ability is considered independent of learning, experience, and education.

concepts.name: focus
concepts.definition: The center of attention or concentration.

concepts.name: focused attention
concepts.definition: the ability to respond discretely to specific visual, auditory or tactile stimuli.

concepts.name: form perception
concepts.definition: the sensory discrimination of a pattern, shape or outline.

concepts.name: functional fixedness
concepts.definition: a cognitive bias that limits a person to using an object only in the way it is traditionally used.

concepts.name: gaze
concepts.definition: The act of fixating the eyes onto a location.

concepts.name: generalization
concepts.definition: The act of transferring knowledge learned from one event to a novel event that is similar in some respect.

concepts.name: generic knowledge
concepts.definition: Generic knowledge is knowledge that is applicable not just to a single entity but to a class of entities.

concepts.name: gestalt
concepts.definition: a collection of physical, biological, psychological or symbolic entities that creates a unified concept, configuration or pattern which is greater than the sum of its parts (of a character, personality, or being).

concepts.name: goal
concepts.definition: The desired end-point of behavior(s).

concepts.name: goal formation
concepts.definition: The processes that create and maintain representations of goal states.

concepts.name: goal maintenance
concepts.definition: The maintenance of information regarding task goals in working memory.

concepts.name: goal management
concepts.definition: consists of the process of recognizing or inferring goals, abandoning no longer relevant goals, identifying and resolving conflicts among goals, and prioritizing goals consistently for optimal success.

concepts.name: goal state
concepts.definition: A point reached when goal directed behavior has successfully concluded.

concepts.name: gustatory learning
concepts.definition: The formation of a knowledge representation that contains information about gustatory percepts.

concepts.name: gustatory memory
concepts.definition: the cognitive capacity of storing and retrieving information related to taste.

concepts.name: gustatory perception
concepts.definition: The processes involved with representing gustatory sensations as such.

concepts.name: habit
concepts.definition: An acquired pattern of behavior that often occurs automatically and is reliably triggered by some event or stimulus.

concepts.name: habit learning
concepts.definition: The process of acquiring a habit

concepts.name: habit memory
concepts.definition: the memory representation of a learned habit, generally thought to be represented as a stimulus-response association

concepts.name: hallucination
concepts.definition: in the broadest sense of the word, is a perception in the absence of a stimulus. In a stricter sense, hallucinations are defined as perceptions in a conscious and awake state in the absence of external stimuli which have qualities of real perception, in that they are vivid, substantial, and located in external objective space.

concepts.name: hedonism
concepts.definition: a school which argues that pleasure is the only intrinsic good, often used as a justification for evaluating actions in terms of how much pleasure and how little pain (i.e. suffering) they produce.

concepts.name: heuristic search
concepts.definition: refers to experience-based techniques for problem solving, learning, and discovery. Heuristic methods are used to speed up the process of finding a good enough solution, where an exhaustive search is impractical. Examples of this method include using a "rule of thumb", an educated guess, an intuitive judgment, or common sense.  In more precise terms, heuristics are strategies using readily accessible, though loosely applicable, information to control problem solving in human beings and machines

concepts.name: hill climbing
concepts.definition: A fast but sometimes unreliable optimization method.  When searching for the minimum/maximum value of a function a random step is taken; if the value improves it replaces the current value, then another random step is taken.

concepts.name: humiliation
concepts.definition: to reduce to a lower position in one's own eyes or others' eyes.

concepts.name: humor
concepts.definition: the tendency of particular cognitive experiences to provoke laughter  and provide amusement.

concepts.name: iconic memory
concepts.definition: very brief sensory memory of some visual stimuli, that occur in the form of mental pictures.

concepts.name: imageability
concepts.definition: is a property of a word or concept reflecting how easy or difficult it is to visually or acoustically imagine.

concepts.name: imagery
concepts.definition: an experience that, on most occasions, significantly resembles the experience of perceiving some object, event, or scene, but occurs when the relevant object, event, or scene is not actually present to the senses.

concepts.name: implicit knowledge
concepts.definition: knowledge that is kept in a personâs mind without necessarily being expressed in words and is often acted on instinctively.

concepts.name: implicit learning
concepts.definition: None

concepts.name: implicit memory
concepts.definition: Type of memory in which experiences increases performance of task without one's conscious awareness of these previous experiences. This type of memory applies to habit learning, skills, conditioning.

concepts.name: imprinting
concepts.definition: a rapid learning process that takes place early in the life of a social animal and establishes a behavior pattern (as recognition of and attraction to its own kind or a substitute).

concepts.name: inattention
concepts.definition: The failure to process an external stimulus (often refers to sensory stimuli).

concepts.name: incidental learning
concepts.definition: Learning without explicit knowledge of doing so, but occurring through interaction with the environment (e.g., by observation/copying of behavior or response to reinforcement).

concepts.name: incubation
concepts.definition: the process of thinking about a problem subconsciously while being involved in other activities

concepts.name: indignation
concepts.definition: anger aroused by something unjust, unworthy, or mean.

concepts.name: induction
concepts.definition: reaching a conclusion from a set of premises that could, but do not necessarily, lead to it

concepts.name: inductive reasoning
concepts.definition: reasoning from a specific case or cases and deriving a general rule, drawing inferences from observations in order to make generalizations.

concepts.name: inference
concepts.definition: the act of passing from one proposition, statement, or judgment considered as true to another whose truth is believed to follow from that of the former; the act of passing from statistical sample data to generalizations (as of the value of population parameters) usually with calculated degrees of certainty.

concepts.name: inhibition
concepts.definition: The process by which a response or thought is suppressed.

concepts.name: inhibition of return
concepts.definition: the phenomenon in which the speed and accuracy with which an object is detected are first briefly enhanced (for perhaps 100-300 milliseconds) after the object is attended, and then detection speed and accuracy are impaired (for perhaps 500-3000 milliseconds).

concepts.name: insight
concepts.definition: In problem solving, the moment at which an underlying relation between cause and effect is discovered/identified.

concepts.name: instinct
concepts.definition: a natural or inherent aptitude, impulse, or capacity; a largely inheritable and unalterable tendency of an organism to make a complex and specific response to environmental stimuli without involving reason, behavior that is mediated by reactions below the conscious level.

concepts.name: instrumental conditioning
concepts.definition: a learning process in which the consequences of an action are used to modify aspects of that action thereafter; these aspects include form and frequency (including the likelihood of reoccurrence at all).

concepts.name: instrumental learning
concepts.definition: learning based on reward; a form of learning that takes place as a direct consequence of a reward or pleasant outcome for the learner.

concepts.name: integration
concepts.definition: coordination of mental processes into a normal effective personality or with the individual's environment

concepts.name: intelligence
concepts.definition: the ability to learn or understand or to deal with new or trying situations; the skilled use of reason; the ability to apply knowledge to manipulate one's environment or to think abstractly as measured by objective criteria

concepts.name: intention
concepts.definition: an act or instance of determining mentally upon some action or result; meaning or significance.

concepts.name: intentional forgetting
concepts.definition: the purposeful forgetting of information that is no longer needed.

concepts.name: intentional learning
concepts.definition: learning that is motivated  with intention and is usually goal directed.

concepts.name: intentionality
concepts.definition: the state of having or being formed by an intention; (philosophy) the property of being about or directed toward a subject, as inherent in conscious states, beliefs, or creations of the mind, such as sentences or books.

concepts.name: interference
concepts.definition: the disturbing effect of new information on the other information with which it is inconsistent

concepts.name: intermediate-term memory
concepts.definition: a specialized term referring for information about a current task.

concepts.name: internal speech
concepts.definition: also known as inner voice, internal speech, or verbal stream of consciousness is thinking in words. It also refers to the semi-constant internal monologue one has with oneself at a conscious or semi-conscious level.

concepts.name: interrogative
concepts.definition: of, pertaining to, or conveying a question.

concepts.name: intonation
concepts.definition: the ability to play or sing notes in tune; manner of utterance, specifically the rise and fall in pitch of the voice in speech.

concepts.name: intrinsic motivation
concepts.definition: a highly desired form of incentive that stems from a person's internal desire for self-satisfaction or pleasure in performing the task itself.

concepts.name: introspection
concepts.definition: the self-observation and reporting of conscious inner thoughts, desires  and sensations. It is a conscious mental and usually purposive process relying on thinking, reasoning, and examining one's own thoughts, feelings.

concepts.name: involuntary attention
concepts.definition: results when the conscious mind changes focus to sudden changes in the environment (big sound, intensity of light, unique situation etc.).  The person is not prepared for the attention and the attention is not under control of the individual.  The persons attention is less concerned with motives, interests, and needs and the stimulus is usually more important than any functional factors.

concepts.name: irony
concepts.definition: a situation, literary technique, or rhetorical device, in which there is an incongruity or discordance that goes strikingly beyond the most simple and evident meaning of words or actions.

concepts.name: judgment
concepts.definition: the process of forming an opinion or evaluation by discerning and comparing

concepts.name: kinaesthetic representation
concepts.definition: is a representation of sensory inputs from muscles, tendons, and joints (e.g.,the joint angles used to reach a point in space).

concepts.name: kinesthesia
concepts.definition: a sense mediated by receptors located in muscles, tendons, and joints and stimulated by bodily movements and tensions.

concepts.name: knowledge
concepts.definition: information acquired and represented by a person through experience or education

concepts.name: language
concepts.definition: The mental ability to encode and decode information, and translate this information into verbal, acoustic and visual representations, according to a set of rules that are common across a population.

concepts.name: language comprehension
concepts.definition: The ability to understand communication from others, such as speech, written text, gestures, or sign language.

concepts.name: language learning
concepts.definition: the process by which humans acquire the capacity to perceive, produce and use words to understand and communicate, this capacity involves the picking up of diverse capacities including syntax, phonetics, and an extensive vocabulary, the language might be vocal as with speech or manual as in sign.

concepts.name: language production
concepts.definition: is translating a concept or set of ideas into spoken, signed or written form

concepts.name: learning
concepts.definition: The process of acquiring new skills/knowledge/information

concepts.name: lemma
concepts.definition: an abstract form of a word before any phonological assignment, arising early in speech production

concepts.name: lexical encoding
concepts.definition: converting vocabulary, words, or morphemes of a language into a code.

concepts.name: lexical retrieval
concepts.definition: retrieval of a lexical entry

concepts.name: lexicon
concepts.definition: The vocabulary of a language, including its words and expressions.

concepts.name: linguistic competence
concepts.definition: a speaker's implicit, internalized knowledge of the rules of their language.

concepts.name: listening
concepts.definition: to pay attention to sound; to hear something with thoughtful attention, give consideration; to be alert to catch an expected sound.

concepts.name: logic
concepts.definition: a science that deals with the principles and criteria of validity of inference and demonstration; the science of the formal principles of reasoning.

concepts.name: logical reasoning
concepts.definition: The strategy when  one uses deduction, induction, or abduction to evaluate preconditions and rules to determnie a conclusion.

concepts.name: long-term memory
concepts.definition: a system for permanently storing, managing, and retrieving information for later use, items of information stored as long-term memory may be available for a lifetime.

concepts.name: loss aversion
concepts.definition: The tendency of individuals to be more sensitive to the possibility of losing objects or money than they are to the possibility of gaining the same objects or amounts of money.

concepts.name: lying
concepts.definition: the expression of a falsehood

concepts.name: mathematical reasoning
concepts.definition: Reasoning about mathematical objects

concepts.name: meaning
concepts.definition: the connotation of a word or phrase

concepts.name: mechanical reasoning
concepts.definition: Reasoning about mechanical objects or functions

concepts.name: melody
concepts.definition: a linear succession of musical tones which is perceived as a single entity.

concepts.name: memory
concepts.definition: The ability of an organism to use past events to inform/influence current actions

concepts.name: mental arithmetic
concepts.definition: mathematical calculations done mentally, without writing them down.

concepts.name: mental imagery
concepts.definition: is an experience that, on most occasions, significantly resembles the experience of perceiving (through any of the senses) of some object, event, or scene, but occurs when the relevant object, event, or scene is not actually present to the senses.

concepts.name: mental representation
concepts.definition: a presentation to the mind in the form of an idea or image.

concepts.name: mental rotation
concepts.definition: Ability to rotate an object in one's mind; ability to make perceptual judgments on a new spatial configuration of an object.

concepts.name: metacognition
concepts.definition: awareness or analysis of one's own learning or thinking processes.

concepts.name: metacognitive skill
concepts.definition: a learners' automatic awareness of their own knowledge and their ability to understand, control, and manipulate their own cognitive processes.

concepts.name: metaphor
concepts.definition: a figure of speech in which a word or phrase literally denoting one kind of object or idea is used in place of another to suggest a likeness or analogy between them.

concepts.name: misattribution
concepts.definition: attributing an event to something with which it has no connection or association.

concepts.name: monitoring
concepts.definition: the act of checking for particular kinds of information

concepts.name: mood
concepts.definition: a conscious state of mind or predominant emotion.

concepts.name: motor control
concepts.definition: The function of supervising motor activities

concepts.name: motor learning
concepts.definition: the process of improving motor skills, the smoothness and accuracy of movements.

concepts.name: motor planning
concepts.definition: the conception of a future motoric action

concepts.name: motor program
concepts.definition: abstract representation of a movement

concepts.name: motor sequence learning
concepts.definition: The acquisition of knowledge regarding sequences of motor action

concepts.name: movement
concepts.definition: change of place or position or posture

concepts.name: naming
concepts.definition: the expression of the name of an object

concepts.name: narrative
concepts.definition: a story that is created in a constructive format (as a work of writing, speech, poetry, prose, pictures, song, motion pictures, video games, theater or dance) that describes a sequence of fictional or non-fictional events.

concepts.name: navigation
concepts.definition: The process of controlling the movement of a body/entity/vehicle through space from one point to another.

concepts.name: nociception
concepts.definition: the processes of encoding and processing noxious stimuli.

concepts.name: nondeclarative knowledge
concepts.definition: The nonconscious or implicit ability to express and practice learned information.

concepts.name: nondeclarative memory
concepts.definition: Memory acquired through experience and which can not be consciously articulated (such as by recall or recognition). This type of memory includes priming, conditioning, skill-acquisition, and habits.

concepts.name: novelty detection
concepts.definition: the identification of new or unknown information

concepts.name: object categorization
concepts.definition: the assignment of an object to a particular category

concepts.name: object centered representation
concepts.definition: In an object-centered representation, the position of the subparts of an object are encoded with respect to a set of axes and an origin centered on the object. Several physiological and neuropsychological results support the existence of such representations in humans and monkeys. An explicit representation would involve neurons with invariant response properties in object-centered coordinates.

concepts.name: object detection
concepts.definition: deals with detecting instances of semantic objects of a certain class (such as humans, buildings, cars, etc.).

concepts.name: object manipulation
concepts.definition: is a form of dexterity play or performance in which one or more artists physically interact with props such as balls, hoops, rings, poi, staff, devil sticks, or clubs. Object manipulation can be considered an advanced combinatorial form of sports, dance, and games.

concepts.name: object perception
concepts.definition: The process of transforming basic visual sensory input (such as contrast, edge, motion, color etc) into a more abstract and semantically identifiable whole.

concepts.name: object recognition
concepts.definition: is the ability to perceive an objectâs physical properties (such as shape, colour and texture) and apply semantic attributes to the object, which includes the understanding of its use, previous experience with the object and how it relates to others.

concepts.name: olfaction
concepts.definition: the sense of smell; the act or process of smelling.

concepts.name: olfactory perception
concepts.definition: the sensation that results when olfactory receptors in the nose are stimulated by particular chemicals in gaseous form.

concepts.name: orthographic lexicon
concepts.definition: A set of representations of orthographic information

concepts.name: parsing
concepts.definition: to resolve (as a sentence) into component parts of speech and describe them grammatically

concepts.name: passive attention
concepts.definition: refers to the involuntary process directed by external events that stand out from their environment, such as a bright flash, a strong odor, or a sudden loud noise.

concepts.name: past tense
concepts.definition: refers to a form of a verb that indicates that the action already has occurred

concepts.name: pattern recognition
concepts.definition: The process of identifying a meaningful pattern in raw data.

concepts.name: pavlovian conditioning
concepts.definition: a form of learning in which a stimulus (designated the "conditional stimulus" or CS and being one without inherent significance) is paired with an unconditional stimulus or US, so named because it is biologically significant (e.g. food, sex, drug, pain), until the participant responds to the former in a way that conveys its association of the two. Importantly, participant response may be different between the US and its paired CS.

concepts.name: perception
concepts.definition: the conscious experience or mental registration of a sensory stimulus

concepts.name: perceptual binding
concepts.definition: is the cognitive ability to couple characteristics between items that one is perceiving.  This can be illustrated by the one observing a blue square and a yellow circle.  Through the neural mechanisms of perceptual binding, one can ensure that the sensing of blue is coupled to that of a square shape and that of yellow is coupled to that of a circle.

concepts.name: perceptual categorization
concepts.definition: A selective system that can have no a priori information about the particular stimuli that might be encountered in its environment, other than boundary conditions implicit in the construction of its recognizing elements. Perceptual categorization, according to this view, does not involve the "reading in" of readily available information about the stimulus category; rather, it involves the utilization of multiple cues in degenerate, overlapping sets and under the influence of context.

concepts.name: perceptual fluency
concepts.definition: is the ease at which the brain can process information.

concepts.name: perceptual identification
concepts.definition: has two different processing stages.  The first stage yields a state of of perceptual information about the stimulus presented.  The second stage is the processing of attained perceptual information in a response.

concepts.name: perceptual learning
concepts.definition: long lasting improvement in performing perceptual  (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory or taste) tasks as a function of experience.

concepts.name: perceptual similarity
concepts.definition: Perceptual similarity is the subjective similarity between two stimuli as perceived by the observer. Thus, object A may be rated as more similar to object B than to object C despite a greater difference in some physical metric (such as height or width) between objects A and C than between objects A and B. This may differ across modalities: for example, two objects may be rated as more similar when seen than when touched. However, the physical, objective similarity between the two objects remains the same regardless of which modality is used to explore them.

concepts.name: perceptual skill
concepts.definition: The ability to observe and understand the events surrounding an individual.

concepts.name: performance monitoring
concepts.definition: the online evaluation of one's performance on a task

concepts.name: phonation
concepts.definition: process by which the vocal folds produce certain sounds through quasi-periodic vibration; any oscillatory state of any part of the larynx that modifies the airstream.

concepts.name: phonological buffer
concepts.definition: a passive storage device that is part of the articulatory rehearsal loop; serves as a part of the mechanisms ordinarily needed for hearing.  In rehearsal, the buffer is loaded by means of subvocalization.

concepts.name: phonological code
concepts.definition: A representation of information using phonological features

concepts.name: phonological encoding
concepts.definition: involves retrieval of segmental and supra-segmental information and the generation of a syllabified phonological word, and the computation of the phonetic form of the intended utterance, referred to as phonetic encoding.

concepts.name: phonological retrieval
concepts.definition: The retrieval of phonological representations based on other cues

concepts.name: phonological working memory
concepts.definition: The process of maintaining sound information online for a limited amount of time.

concepts.name: planning
concepts.definition: formulation, evaluation and selection of a sequence of actions to achieve a desired goal.

concepts.name: pragmatic inference
concepts.definition: Inferences are made when a person (or machine) goes beyond available evidence to form a conclusion. A pragmatic inference (also known as an inductive inference) is one which is likely to be true because of the state of the world. Unlike deductive inferences, pragmatic (inductive) inferences do yield conclusions that increase the semantic information over and above that found in the initial premises.

concepts.name: pragmatic knowledge
concepts.definition: is how individuals communicate meaning and how they produce contextually appropriate utterances, sentences, or texts.  Pragmatic knowledge includes sociolinguistic and functional knowledge.

concepts.name: pragmatic reasoning
concepts.definition: Pragmatic reasoning is defined as the process of finding the intended meaning(s) of the given, and it is suggested that this amounts to the process of inferring the appropriate context(s) in which to interpret the given.

concepts.name: preattentive processing
concepts.definition: background activity that necessarily precedes conscious mental activity; major purpose is the preparation of sensory input for use in focal-attentive processes including encoding of the basic properties of sensory input.

concepts.name: preconscious perception
concepts.definition: is the subthreshold process of visual perception.

concepts.name: prejudice
concepts.definition: preconceived judgment or opinion; an adverse opinion or leaning formed without just grounds or before sufficient knowledge; an irrational attitude of hostility directed against an individual, a group, a race, or their supposed characteristics.

concepts.name: primary memory
concepts.definition: the temporary maintenance system for conscious processing of information.

concepts.name: proactive interference
concepts.definition: the forgetting of information due to interference from the traces of events or learning that occurred prior to the materials to be remembered; occurs when in any given context, past memories inhibit an individualâs full potential to retain new memories.

concepts.name: problem solving
concepts.definition: Broadly, the mental processes involved in finding a solution to a problem.

concepts.name: procedural knowledge
concepts.definition: Knowledge exercised in the performance of a task/activity. Its acquisition or structure is often unavailable to the actor.

concepts.name: procedural learning
concepts.definition: The acquisition of a skill or ability through practice which is not accessible to verbalization or conscious awareness.

concepts.name: procedural memory
concepts.definition: memory for how to do things; procedural memories are automatically retrieved and utilized for the execution of the step-by-step procedures involved in both cognitive and motor skills.

concepts.name: procedural rule
concepts.definition: No definition submitted yet

concepts.name: processing capacity
concepts.definition: No definition submitted yet

concepts.name: processing stage
concepts.definition: A subset of mental operations that are confined some feature space of information within a stream and/or hierarchy of mental operations.

concepts.name: pronunciation
concepts.definition: the way a word or a language is spoken, or the manner in which someone utters a word.

concepts.name: proper noun
concepts.definition: A subject that usually indicates a particular person, place, or object.

concepts.name: proprioception
concepts.definition: the sense of the relative position of neighboring parts of the body.

concepts.name: prosodic stress
concepts.definition: the stress and intonation patterns of an utterance.

concepts.name: prosody
concepts.definition: the rhythm, stress, and intonation of speech.

concepts.name: prospective memory
concepts.definition: remembering to perform an intended action...prospective memory is self-initiated and does not operate directly on external stimuli.

concepts.name: prospective planning
concepts.definition: No definition submitted yet

concepts.name: prototype
concepts.definition: A most common, standard or basic mental representation of some category.

concepts.name: quantitative skill
concepts.definition: the ability to to use mathematical concepts to solve problems.

concepts.name: reading
concepts.definition: Decoding symbols to derive their meaning.

concepts.name: reasoning
concepts.definition: drawing of inferences or conclusions through the use of reason.

concepts.name: regret
concepts.definition: an emotional response to remembrance of a past state, condition, or experience that one wishes had been different

concepts.name: relational learning
concepts.definition: learning to differentiate among stimuli on the basis of relational properties (e.g., the larger of two stimuli) rather than absolute properties (e.g., the stimulus that has a given size).

concepts.name: remote memory
concepts.definition: memory for events of long ago as opposed to recent events.

concepts.name: repressed memory
concepts.definition: A memory (often traumatic) that is unavailable for recall.

concepts.name: resource limit
concepts.definition: the maximum amount of cognitive resources that can be allocated to various, often competing tasks

concepts.name: resource sharing
concepts.definition: is a unique characteristic of humans and several primates that involve sharing resources such as food, shelter, etc., as a collective risk-reduction against variability in resource supply.

concepts.name: response inhibition
concepts.definition: Suppression of actions that are inappropriate in a given context and that interfere with goal-driven behavior.

concepts.name: response selection
concepts.definition: The selection of one action from a limited set of possible actions.

concepts.name: retention
concepts.definition:
a preservation of the aftereffects of experience and learning that makes recall or recognition possible.
Persistence of learned behavior or experience during a period when it is not being performed o r practiced.
Retention is the second stage of memory after encoding and before retrival

concepts.name: retrieval
concepts.definition:
The process of accessing information from memory or other storage devices; the possibility of recovery, restoration, or rectification.
Retrieval is the third stage of memory after encoding and retention.

concepts.name: retrieval cue
concepts.definition: An event or experience that facilitates retrieval of information from long-term memory because of its association to that information.

concepts.name: retroactive interference
concepts.definition: impeded retrieval and performance of previously learnt information due to newly acquired and practiced information.

concepts.name: rhythm
concepts.definition: Movement marked by the regulated succession of strong and weak elements, or of opposite or different conditions.  While rhythm most commonly applies to sound, such as music and spoken language, it may also refer to visual presentation, as timed movement through space.

concepts.name: risk
concepts.definition:
Formally and mathematically speaking, the minimal definition of risk is what (Rothschild and Stiglitz, 1970) call a mean-preserving increase in dispersion. A typical example is a gamble offering $400 or $600 based on the outcome of a coin flip (i.e. with equal probability (50%)); this is less risky as compared to a similar gamble offering $200 or $800 [again depending on the outcome of a coin flip]. Notice here that the mean outcome (or âexpected valueâ) remains the same for both gambles.

Thus risk can increase by keeping both the probabilities and the expected value the same. 

There are other approaches to risk that are less mathematically stringent but have higher ecological validity. For instance increasing the probability of a (positive outcome) is associated with a reduced perception of risk. Notice though now that the expected value (or the mean outcome) also increases. So, it is difficult in that case to disentangle the two metrics.

Many times  the term risk is associated with the probability of a negative outcome, or what is formally called downside risk. This idea is mostly due to the way actuarial science and insurance companies (which are more interested in the negative aspects of risk) use the term. For instance, the statement, ânow we increase the risk,â might be translated as taking more perilous actions, but formally, this is not the case. The point of risk is that the opportunity also increases (âupsideâ risk). Thus, a situation that is riskier can be attractive, especially if the agent focuses on the positive outcomes.

Another approach is the so-called âmoment-basedâ approach. Here, one is interested in the second or higher moments of a distribution, roughly corresponding to variance, skewness and kurtosis. Skewness is of particular interest because it seems that risk-seeking persons (gamblers) can be attracted by positively skewed outcomes. Bets that offer a small probability of a high outcome are  attractive to gamblers (Garrett and Sobel, 1999).

Overall, risk is not a unitary concept and should be very carefully defined.

Note that the term risk as used here should be distinguished from the way the term is used in sentences such as "risk of developing Parkinson's disease". An epidemiologist could help on the definition in that context.

Input by other contributors:
the probability or likelihood that an event will occur; possibility of loss or injury; someone or something that creates or suggests a hazard; the chance that an investment will lose value.

concepts.name: route knowledge
concepts.definition: is represented as a series of directions to follow to get from one place to another.

concepts.name: routine
concepts.definition: a regular course of procedure; habitual or mechanical performance of an established procedure; a reiterated speech or formula; a sequence of computer instructions for performing a particular task.

concepts.name: rule
concepts.definition: a method for performing a psychological operation

concepts.name: rule learning
concepts.definition: process in which a participant gradually acquires knowledge about a fixed but unstated standard that defines, for example, the acceptability of a response or membership of category

concepts.name: sadness
concepts.definition: an emotion  characterized by feelings of unhappiness, disadvantage, loss, and helplessness.

concepts.name: salience
concepts.definition: a parameter of a stimulus that indexes its effectiveness.

concepts.name: schema
concepts.definition: a structured representation that includes a particular organized way of perceiving and responding to a complex situation or set of stimuli.

concepts.name: search
concepts.definition: to look into or over carefully or thoroughly in an effort to find or discover something; to look through or explore by inspecting possible places of concealment or investigating suspicious circumstances; to look at as if to discover or penetrate intention or nature; to uncover, find, or come to know by inquiry or scrutiny.

concepts.name: selective attention
concepts.definition: When multiple external sensory inputs are present, the process of dedicating cognitive and perceptual resources to one type/set of input and attenuating receptiveness to other inputs.

concepts.name: self monitoring
concepts.definition: monitoring of one's own behavior.

concepts.name: semantic category
concepts.definition: is a grouping of vocabulary within a language, organizing words which are interrelated and define each other in various ways. Also referred to as a semantic field.

concepts.name: semantic knowledge
concepts.definition: long-established knowledge about objects, facts, and word meanings.

concepts.name: semantic memory
concepts.definition: refers to one's conceptual knowledge and includes the meanings of words, factual information about the world, and other information not related to specific events or episodes

concepts.name: semantic working memory
concepts.definition: Working memory for meaning

concepts.name: sensory memory
concepts.definition: brief storage of sensory information in each of the senses, which temporarily holds material (e.g., a perceptual experience) for recoding into another memory (such as short-term memory) or for comprehension.

concepts.name: sequence learning
concepts.definition: learning of a sequence of items or responses in the precise order of their presentation.

concepts.name: serial learning
concepts.definition: The process of acquiring information in sequence and following an order that must be preserved at recall.

concepts.name: serial processing
concepts.definition: information processing in which only one sequence of processing operations is carried on at a time.

concepts.name: serial search
concepts.definition: The process of identifying a target within a set of candidate elements by testing the identity of each element against the identity of the sought after target one at a time.

concepts.name: shallow processing
concepts.definition: a mode of thinking in which one pays attention only to appearances and other superficial aspects of the material, typically leading to poor memory retention.

concepts.name: shame
concepts.definition: a painful emotion caused by consciousness of guilt, shortcoming, or impropriety; a condition of humiliating disgrace or disrepute; something that brings censure or reproach.

concepts.name: short-term memory
concepts.definition: A limited-capacity and short-lasting representation of information in the mind. The duration of short-term memory is on the order of seconds, while its capacity is on the order of 4 to 9 independent items.

concepts.name: skepticism
concepts.definition: an attitude of doubt or a disposition to incredulity either in general or toward a particular object.

concepts.name: skill
concepts.definition: Proficiency, facility, or dexterity that is acquired or developed through training or experience.

concepts.name: skill acquisition
concepts.definition: The process of learning to perform a task or set of tasks with increasing facility. Typically implies the formation of procedural (as distinct from semantic or episodic) memories.

concepts.name: social cognition
concepts.definition: the encoding, storage, retrieval, and processing, in the brain, of information relating to conspecifics, or members of the same species.

concepts.name: social context
concepts.definition: the identical or similar social positions and social roles as a whole that influence the individuals of a group.

concepts.name: social intelligence
concepts.definition: the ability to function successfully in interpersonal situations.

concepts.name: somatosensation
concepts.definition: the components of the central and peripheral nervous systems that receive and interpret sensory information from organs in the joints, ligaments, muscles, and skin. This system processes information about the length, degree of stretch, tension, and contraction of muscles; pain; temperature; pressure; and joint position.

concepts.name: source memory
concepts.definition: the episodic source from which a specific item was acquired (e.g., from a person, a book, or television (Schacter, Kaszniak, Kihlstrom, & Valdiserri, 1991, p. 559).

concepts.name: source monitoring
concepts.definition: The process of identifying the the source or context at acquisition of information that has been stored in memory.

concepts.name: spatial ability
concepts.definition: skill in perceiving the visual world, transforming and modifying initial perceptions, and mentally recreating spatial aspects of one's visual experience without the relevant stimuli.

concepts.name: spatial attention
concepts.definition: The allocation or prioritization of mental resources based on spatial coordinates (with respect to the body, head etc).
