concepts.name: spatial cognition
concepts.definition: the acquisition, organization, utilization, and revision of knowledge about spatial environments.

concepts.name: spatial memory
concepts.definition: the part of memory  responsible for recording information about one's environment and its spatial orientation.

concepts.name: spatial working memory
concepts.definition: The ability to maintain online information that relates to space. This process has limited capacity and its contents are not stored permanently.

concepts.name: speech perception
concepts.definition: the process by which the sounds of language are heard, interpreted and understood.

concepts.name: speech processing
concepts.definition: the processing of speech signals

concepts.name: speech production
concepts.definition: is the process by which spoken words are selected to be produced, have their phonetics formulated and then finally are articulated by the motor system in the vocal apparatus. Speech production can be spontaneous such as when a person creates the words of a conversation, reaction such as when they name a picture or read aloud a written word, or a vocal imitation such as in speech repetition.  Speech production is not the same as language production since language can also be produced manually by signs.

concepts.name: spreading activation
concepts.definition: a method for searching associative networks, neural networks, or semantic networks; the search process is initiated by labeling a set of source nodes (e.g. concepts in a semantic network) with weights or "activation" and then iteratively propagating or "spreading" that activation out to other nodes linked to the source nodes.

concepts.name: stereopsis
concepts.definition: the process in visual perception leading to the sensation of depth from the two slightly different projections of the world onto the retinas of the two eyes.

concepts.name: stereotypes
concepts.definition: something conforming to a fixed or general pattern; a standardized mental picture that is held in common by members of a group and that represents an oversimplified opinion, prejudiced attitude, or uncritical judgment.

concepts.name: strategy
concepts.definition: A plan of action designed to achieve a particular goal.

concepts.name: stress
concepts.definition: refers to the consequence of the failure of an organism â human or animal â to respond appropriately to emotional or physical threats, whether actual or imagined.

concepts.name: sublexical route
concepts.definition: is a theoretical component of Coltheart's dual-route reading model that refers to using spelling-to-sound correspondences to convert a written word (i.e. orthography) into a spoken word (i.e. phonology).  In other words, it is the route by which letters are linked to their sounds and the sounds are assembled into a whole word pronunciation.  It complements the lexical route where the whole word is recognized and linked to its sound.

concepts.name: subliminal perception
concepts.definition:
a visual or auditory message that is allegedly perceived psychologically, but not consciously;
occurs when a stimulus is too weak to be perceived yet a person is influenced by it.

concepts.name: supervisory attentional system
concepts.definition: a loosely defined collection of brain processes that are responsible for planning, cognitive flexibility, abstract thinking, rule acquisition, initiating appropriate actions and inhibiting inappropriate actions, and selecting relevant sensory information.

concepts.name: surprise
concepts.definition: a brief emotional state that is the result of experiencing an unexpected relevant event.

concepts.name: sustained attention
concepts.definition: the ability to maintain a consistent behavioral response during continuous and repetitive activity.

concepts.name: syntactic parsing
concepts.definition: the way that human beings, rather than computers, analyze a sentence or phrase (in spoken language or text) in terms of grammatical constituents, identifying the parts of speech, syntactic relations, etc.

concepts.name: syntactic processing
concepts.definition: processing of the structural and grammatical aspects of language

concepts.name: syntax
concepts.definition: the processing of elements (e.g. linguistic elements, like words) that are grouped to form constituents in a connected or orderly manner (e.g. phrases or clauses), implying an harmonious arrangement of such elements.

concepts.name: taste aversion
concepts.definition: occurs when the taste of a certain food is associated with symptoms caused by a toxic, spoiled, or poisonous substance;  generally caused after ingestion of the food causes nausea, sickness, or vomiting. The ability to develop a taste aversion is considered an adaptive trait or survival mechanism that trains the body to avoid poisonous substances (e.g., poisonous berries) before they can cause harm.

concepts.name: text comprehension
concepts.definition: Intentional thinking during which meaning is constructed through interactions between text and reader.

concepts.name: text processing
concepts.definition: The handling of alphabetic characters

concepts.name: theory of mind
concepts.definition: the ability for a person to connect emotional states to themselves and others and understand that other people may have different  beliefs, desires, or intentions from one's self.  It is intimately connected with the development of a person's ability to analyze and interpret the intentions of others.

concepts.name: thermosensation
concepts.definition: the sensory perception of thermal stimuli.

concepts.name: top down processing
concepts.definition: perceptions formed by starting with the larger concept or idea, then working down to the finer details of that concept or idea.

concepts.name: traumatic memory
concepts.definition: A type of memory results from trauma experience, such as a natural disaster or violent events.

concepts.name: uncertainty
concepts.definition: the lack of knowledge regarding the likelihood of potential outcomes

concepts.name: unconscious process
concepts.definition: a mental process that you are not directly aware of.

concepts.name: utility
concepts.definition: a measure of the subjective worth of an outcome.

concepts.name: valence
concepts.definition: the degree of attractiveness an individual, activity, or thing possesses as a behavioral goal.

concepts.name: verbal fluency
concepts.definition: the ability to rapidly access your mental vocabulary while talking or writing.

concepts.name: verbal memory
concepts.definition: Recall based on spoken words.

concepts.name: visual attention
concepts.definition: two-stage process in which attention is distributed uniformly over the external visual scene and processing of information is performed in parallel, attention is then concentrated to a specific area of the visual scene (i.e. it is focused), and processing is performed in a serial fashion.

concepts.name: visual buffer
concepts.definition: a short-term memory store for visual information

concepts.name: visual imagery
concepts.definition: an experience that, on most occasions, significantly resembles the experience of perceiving some object, event, or scene, but occurs when the relevant object, event, or scene is not actually present to the senses.

concepts.name: visual masking
concepts.definition: the reduction or elimination of the visibility of a brief a target stimulus by the presentation of a second stimulus (the mask) contiguous in space and/or time

concepts.name: visual memory
concepts.definition: a part of memory  preserving some characteristics of our senses pertaining to visual experience.

concepts.name: visual object recognition
concepts.definition: is the process of identifying an object based on its visual attributes

concepts.name: visual perception
concepts.definition: Visual perception is the ability to interpret the surrounding environment by processing information that is contained in visible light. The resulting perception is also known as eyesight, sight, or vision.

concepts.name: visual representation
concepts.definition: An internal representation of visual information

concepts.name: visual search
concepts.definition: orienting for targets in an array or a natural scene, through both covert and overt shifts in attention; this is different from the visual search task in that it refers to a general phenomenon and not to a paradigm.

concepts.name: visual working memory
concepts.definition: The ability to maintain visual information online for a limited time interval (~ 4 sec). This information is not stored permanently.

concepts.name: visuospatial sketch pad
concepts.definition: The cognitive construct and mental process of temporarily storing visual and spatial information for online use in operations of working memory (c.f., Alan Baddeley) .

concepts.name: wisdom
concepts.definition: accumulated philosophic or scientific learning.

concepts.name: word comprehension
concepts.definition: the ability to understand the meaning of words.

concepts.name: word generation
concepts.definition: The cognitive process of producing words on ones own term instead of extracting them from an outside source.

concepts.name: word order
concepts.definition: is the sequence of the syntactic constituents of a language.

concepts.name: word pronunciation
concepts.definition: is the act or result of producing the sounds of speech, including articulation, stress, and intonation, often with reference to some standard of correctness or acceptability.

concepts.name: word recognition
concepts.definition: the ability of a reader to recognize words correctly and virtually effortlessly.

concepts.name: word repetition
concepts.definition: Overt pronounciation of auditorily presented words

concepts.name: working memory
concepts.definition: active maintenance and flexible updating of goal/task relevant information (items, goals, strategies, etc.) in a form that resists interference but has limited capacity. These representations may involve flexible binding of representations, may be characterized by the absence of external support for the internally maintained representations, and are frequently temporary due to ongoing interference

concepts.name: action initiation
concepts.definition: the facilitation or initiation of an act

concepts.name: attention shift
concepts.definition: The change that occurs when information that is currently active in the mind is replaced by other information. The information content is typically sensory in nature.

concepts.name: attention span
concepts.definition: Amount of time or space that an individual can dedicate to particular task or content without becoming distracted.

concepts.name: attentional focusing
concepts.definition: The ability to focus attention on cues in the environment that are relevant to the task in hand; can also include suppression of distracting stimuli

concepts.name: attention shifting
concepts.definition: The process by which information that is currently relevant in the mind is replaced by other information. This information is typically sensory in nature but may also be semantic.

concepts.name: set shifting
concepts.alias: mental set shifting, task set reconfiguration
concepts.definition: disengagement of an irrelevant task set and subsequent engagement of a relevant task set despite interference and/or priming

concepts.name: task switching
concepts.definition: The process of switching from one task or goal to another, depending on the context or instructions, that is, the process of switching between task sets.

concepts.name: decision
concepts.definition: The outcome of a process during which a choice is made, usually between several possible options

concepts.name: framing
concepts.definition:
Framing is a method of biasing opinions- a framing effect occurs when the description of information, such as a speaker presenting an issue, has an emphasis on a subset of potentially
relevant considerations and causes individuals to focus on these considerations when constructing their opinions.

concepts.name: risk aversion
concepts.definition: None

concepts.name: risk seeking
concepts.definition:
The willingness of an individual to choose an option with a less-than-certain probability of reward over an option with a certain reward of equal or higher expected value. 

BEHAVIORAL PHENOMENA

concepts.name: emotion perception
concepts.definition: The process involving understanding feelings with different valences of oneself or of others

concepts.name: emotion recognition
concepts.definition: The process of assigning an emotion to one of the discrete categories of emotion available in a particular culture.

concepts.name: emotional bonding
concepts.definition: A process of bringing people together based on mutually shared emotions.

concepts.name: empathy
concepts.definition: The act of understanding, being aware of, being sensitive to, and or experiencing the feelings, thoughts, and experience of another.

concepts.name: fear
concepts.definition: A state of high negative emotional arousal triggered by an impending threat (real or imaginary) and generally associated with the flight or fight response. Fear is the activation of the brainâs defensive motivational system to promote behaviors that protect the organism from perceived danger. Normal fear involves a pattern of adaptive responses to conditioned or unconditioned threat stimuli (exteroceptive or interoceptive). Fear can involve internal representations and cognitive processing, and can be modulated by a variety of factors.

concepts.name: frustration
concepts.definition: a deep chronic sense or state of insecurity and dissatisfaction arising from unresolved problems or unfulfilled needs.

concepts.name: grief
concepts.definition: deep and poignant distress caused by or as if by bereavement.

concepts.name: happiness
concepts.definition: a state of mind or feeling characterized by contentment, love, satisfaction, pleasure, or joy.

concepts.name: discourse
concepts.definition: the capacity of orderly thought or procedure, verbal interchange of ideas; formal and orderly and usually extended expression of thought on a subject, connected speech or writing, linguistic unit larger than a sentence.

concepts.name: discourse comprehension
concepts.definition: Discourse comprehension is the act of interpreting a written or spoken message by integrating the incoming information into the memory or knowledge structures of the interpreter.

concepts.name: discourse knowledge
concepts.definition: knowledge regarding discourse

concepts.name: discourse planning
concepts.definition: the formulation of structures, patterns, mental representations, and processes that constitute the written and spoken unit of connected speech or writing longer than a sentence.

concepts.name: discourse processing
concepts.definition: is the cognitive process that investigates the structures, patterns, mental representations, and processes that underlie the written and spoken unit of connected speech or writing longer than a sentence.

concepts.name: discourse production
concepts.definition: the formation of a spoken unit of connected speech or writing longer than a sentence.

concepts.name: grammatical encoding
concepts.definition: the selection of semantically appropriate lexical items and the generation of a syntactic frame or surface form.

concepts.name: grapheme
concepts.definition: a unit (as a letter or digraph) of a writing system; the set of units of a writing system (as letters and letter combinations) that represent a phoneme.

concepts.name: graphemic buffer
concepts.definition: a component dedicated to the temporary storage of abstract orthographic representations prior to their format-specific expression in spelling and/or reading.

concepts.name: illocutionary force
concepts.definition: a speaker's intention in delivering an utterance.

concepts.name: language acquisition
concepts.definition: the process by which humans acquire the capacity to perceive, produce and use words to understand and communicate.

concepts.name: language processing
concepts.definition: the way human beings process speech or writing and understand it as language.

concepts.name: lexical access
concepts.definition: the process by which contact is made with the lexicon on the basis of an initial acoustic-phonetic or phonological representation of some portion of the speech input, the result of lexical success is a cohort of potential word candidates which are compatible with this initial analysis.

concepts.name: lexical ambiguity
concepts.definition: the presence of two or more possible meanings within a single word.

concepts.name: lexical processing
concepts.definition: A general term referring to the processing of single words, typically in the context of visual or auditory word recognition.

concepts.name: morphological processing
concepts.definition: is how the brain registers the patterns of word formation in a particular language, including inflection, derivation, and composition.

concepts.name: morphology
concepts.definition: the structure and content of word forms

concepts.name: orthography
concepts.definition: the representation of the sounds of a language by written or printed symbols; a part of language study that deals with letters and spelling.

concepts.name: phonetics
concepts.definition: the system of speech sounds of a language or group of languages; the study and systematic classification of the sounds made in spoken utterance.

concepts.name: semantic processing
concepts.definition: the cognitive processing of extracting meaning from any form of language (e.g. human language, programming language) as well as formal logics and semiotics

concepts.name: sentence comprehension
concepts.definition: takes place whenever a reader or listener processes a language utterance, either in isolation or in the context of a conversation or a text.

concepts.name: sentence processing
concepts.definition: takes place whenever a reader or listener cognitively processes a language utterance, either in isolation or in the context of a conversation or a text.

concepts.name: sentence production
concepts.definition: The creation and/or utterance of a sentence

concepts.name: active recall
concepts.definition: a principle of efficient learning, which claims the need to actively stimulate memory during the learning process.

concepts.name: active retrieval
concepts.definition: Effortful (volitional) attempt to consciously recollect a memory; often required when retrieval cannot be automatically driven by stimuli.

concepts.name: consolidation
concepts.definition: the process by which a representation becomes stabilized

concepts.name: elaborative rehearsal
concepts.definition: a type of rehearsal proposed by Craik and Lockhart (1972) in their Levels of Processing model of memory. Elaborative rehearsal involves deep semantic processing of a to-be-remembered item resulting in the production of durable memories.

concepts.name: encoding
concepts.definition: The process of creating a new memory trace.

concepts.name: episodic buffer
concepts.definition: A theoretical construct that is part of Alan Baddeley's working memory model and the object of which is to integrate information across sensory domains and communicate with long term memory in the service of working memory.

concepts.name: familiarity
concepts.definition: A quality of memory that is associated with a feeling of knowing that an event has previously occurred, but often not including enough contextual or episodic details sufficient for claiming actual remembering of the event.

concepts.name: forgetting
concepts.definition: The loss of or inability to retrieve a memory.

concepts.name: memory acquisition
concepts.definition: is the process of storage and retrieval of new information in memory.

concepts.name: memory consolidation
concepts.definition: a category of processes that stabilize a memory trace after the initial acquisition.

concepts.name: memory decay
concepts.definition: the loss of memory over time.

concepts.name: memory storage
concepts.definition: The representation of information in the brain in a form that enables potential retrieval at a later time.

concepts.name: memory trace
concepts.definition: A residual, and often decayed, neural representation of previous knowledge or experience.

concepts.name: metamemory
concepts.definition: subjective awareness of and knowledge about memory, and strategies for its effective access and application; includes: awareness of memory contents, different and appropriate memory strategies for particular tasks, and how to use a given memory strategy most effectively.

concepts.name: recall
concepts.definition: The process of retrieving previously stored information, done without the aid of external cues.

concepts.name: recognition
concepts.definition: assigning a detected stimulus into a category (not necessarily task defined)

concepts.name: reconsolidation
concepts.definition: the process of previously consolidated memories being recalled and actively consolidated, it is a distinct process that serves to maintain, strengthen and modify memories that are already stored in the long-term memory.

concepts.name: acuity
concepts.definition: accuracy of perception.

concepts.name: echolocation
concepts.definition: the general method of locating objects by determining the time for an echo to return and the direction from which it returns, used by some animals

concepts.name: edge detection
concepts.definition: a fundamental tool in image processing and computer vision, particularly in the areas of feature detection and feature extraction, which aim at identifying points in a digital image at which the image brightness changes sharply or more formally has discontinuities.

concepts.name: feature detection
concepts.definition: a process of recognizing specific aspects of a stimulus, such as lines, edges, angle, or movement.

concepts.name: figure ground reversal
concepts.definition: Occurs in certain visual illusions (e.g., Vases and Faces or "Rubin's Vase") in which there are multiple valid figure-ground segmentations that can be selected depending on an observer's interpretation.

concepts.name: figure ground segregation
concepts.definition: Discriminating objects from their surroundings by the visual system.

concepts.name: gustation processing
concepts.definition: Form of chemoreception that facilitates taste perception.

concepts.name: memory retrieval
concepts.definition: the process of accessing a stored memory

concepts.name: active maintenance
concepts.definition: The maintenance of information in working memory through active (volitional) rather than passive means

concepts.name: articulatory loop
concepts.definition: one of the subsystems postulated in Alan Baddeleyâs multicomponent model of WORKING MEMORY, specialized for the temporary storage of verbal information.  It consists of a phonological store and an articulatory rehearsal process. The phonological store can hold speech-based information, subject to a rapid decay. The articulatory rehearsal process can refresh the decaying representation by reading it off and feeding it back to the store. It also serves to convert visually presented information (such as written words) into phonological codes and register them into the phonological store.

concepts.name: central executive
concepts.definition: Theoretical 'top-down' cognitive system responsible for the management of executive functions including planning, working memory, attention, problem solving, reasoning, inhibition, multi-tasking, and the initiation and monitoring of actions.

concepts.name: maintenance
concepts.definition: The process of keeping information in active and immediately accessible state.

concepts.name: manipulation
concepts.definition: performance of operations upon information held in working memory

concepts.name: phonological loop
concepts.definition: deals with sound or phonological information and consists of two parts: a short-term phonological store with auditory  memory traces that are subject to rapid decay and an articulatory rehearsal component that can revive the memory traces.

concepts.name: rehearsal
concepts.definition: The repetition of information in an attempt to maintain it longer in memory.

concepts.name: rehearsal loop
concepts.definition: or phonological loop, also called the phonetic loop or the articulatory loop, is the part of working memory that rehearses verbal information. It consists of two parts: a short-term phonological store with auditory memory traces that are subject to rapid decay and an articulatory rehearsal component that can revive the memory traces.The first component is a phonological memory store which can hold traces of acoustic or speech based material. Material in this short term store lasts about two seconds unless it is maintained through the use of the second subcomponent, articulatory subvocal rehearsal. Prevention of articulatory rehearsal results in very rapid forgetting (a process known as decay).

concepts.name: working memory retrieval
concepts.definition: The process of accessing information that is maintained in working memory; the sub-process by which the contents of working memory are accessed.

concepts.name: working memory storage
concepts.definition: The maintenance of information of working memory; a sub-component of working memory that allows for contents of working memory to be retained.

concepts.name: test term
concepts.definition: None

concepts.name: cognitive control
concepts.definition: The top-down modulation of cognitive processes based on higher-order representations such as goals or plans.

concepts.name: echoic memory
concepts.definition: refers to the phenomenon in which there is a brief mental echo that continues to sound after an auditory stimulus has been heard.

concepts.name: reward processing
concepts.definition: A positive return for performance of a specific behavior.

concepts.name: pain
concepts.definition: An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage.

concepts.name: joint attention
concepts.definition: the process of alerting one person to a stimulus through nonverbal cues such as finger pointing or gazing. It is one of the first signs of the development of a theory of mind in babies and serves as an important step to later language and social development.

concepts.name: behavioral inhibition (cognitive)
concepts.definition: Often used as a synonym of "response inhibition" to describe the inhibition of actions.

concepts.name: behavioral inhibition (temperament)
concepts.definition: A temperamental characteristic described by shyness and social anxiety.

concepts.name: central coherence
concepts.definition: a person's ability to understand things in context, frequently described as a deficit in literature on autism

concepts.name: interference resolution
concepts.definition: The process of selecting information with regard to its relevance to an ongoing task and suppressing the processing of irrelevant information.

concepts.name: updating
concepts.definition: The revision or refreshing of information that is maintained in working memory

concepts.name: task set
concepts.definition: The set of rules and/or stimulus-response mappings that define how a task should be performed.

concepts.name: subconscious
concepts.definition:
Subconscious is any neural activity which has the potential to be conscious, but at the moment is processed below the level of consciousness.

In contrast to unconscious information processing, subconscious processing contains meaning (semantic information).

Intuition is a good example for subconscious information processing. In other words, intuition means thinking below the level of consciousness whereby only the output enters the stream of consciousness.

from Peter Walla

concepts.name: semantic information
concepts.definition: information that is not tied to any specific object, event, domain, or application. It includes general factual information about the world (as in an encyclopedia) and oneself.

concepts.name: paraphasia
concepts.definition: generally refers to errors in naming. Collectively, this term is applied to any unintended error of word or sound choice.

concepts.name: phonemic paraphasia
concepts.definition: is the production of unintended sounds or syllables in the utterance of partially recognizable word, e.g., âpakerâ for âpaper.â

concepts.name: neologism
concepts.definition: is the production of nonsense word or words, usually without recognition of errors, e.g., âtableâ becomes âtilto.â

concepts.name: metacomprehension
concepts.definition: refers to the learners' ability to monitor the degree to which they understand information being communicated to them, to recognize failures to comprehend, and to employ repair strategies when failures are identified.

concepts.name: conceptual metaphor
concepts.definition: In cognitive linguistics, metaphor is defined as understanding one conceptual domain in terms of another conceptual domain; for example, using one person's life experience to understand a different person's experience. A conceptual domain can be any coherent organization of experience.

concepts.name: multisensory integration
concepts.definition: The process by which unisensory signals are combined to form a new product. It is operationally defined as a multisensory response (neural or behavioral) that is significantly different from the responses evoked by the modality-specific component stimuli

concepts.name: crossmodal
concepts.definition: A complex of two or more modality-specific [unimodal] stimuli

concepts.name: unisensory
concepts.definition: Describes any sensory process associated with a single sensory modality

concepts.name: multisensory
concepts.definition: a process associated with multiple sensory modalities

concepts.name: synchrony perception
concepts.definition: the process of perceiving whether or not the crossmodal cues (e.g., audio and visual) to an event (e.g., audiovisual speech) are in temporal synchrony with each other.

concepts.name: tactile working memory
concepts.definition: working memory for tactile information

concepts.name: body representation
concepts.definition: A mental representation of one's own body

concepts.name: interoceptive representation
concepts.definition: A representation of the internal state of the body

concepts.name: sense of ownership
concepts.definition: The feeling that something is part of one self.

concepts.name: sense of body ownership
concepts.definition: The feeling that something is part of one's own body.

concepts.name: pain sensitization
concepts.definition: A painful stimulus is perceived more painful over the time course of stimulation.

concepts.name: pain habituation
concepts.definition: A painful stimulus is perceived less painful over the time course of stimulation.

concepts.name: priming
concepts.definition: Priming is the effect of prior exposure to a somehow (e.g. perceptually or semantically) related stimulus on the response to a subsequent stimulus. This effect may be positive and facilitatory (e.g. naming of an object is typically faster when that object has already been recently named) or negative and detrimental (e.g. slower response to a previously ignored stimulus).

concepts.name: expectancy
concepts.definition: A belief about something in the future. Sometimes requires explicit, conscious awareness, distinct from unconscious, conditioning-based learning.

concepts.name: self control
concepts.definition: The effortful control of behaviors, thoughts, or emotions with the aim of increasing the likelihood of attaining long-term over short-term outcomes.

concepts.name: embodied cognition
concepts.definition: a theory emphasizing the essentiality of the body's interaction with the environment to cognition

concepts.name: resource
concepts.definition: any aspect of cognition having bounded availability, eg. memory, attention

concepts.name: curiosity
concepts.definition: wanting knowledge or understanding, often of a novel or unfamiliar entity

concepts.name: imagination
concepts.definition: forming mental images or concepts of what is not actually present to the senses

concepts.name: self talk
concepts.definition: overt verbalisation of thoughts for the purpose of self motivation, problem solving, reasoning, learning or stress management; a behavior commonly witnessed in sports-people during moments of performance pressure

concepts.name: worldview
concepts.definition: overarching subjective account of environmental (ie. that in which an agent is situated) characteristics and functions, applicable across local and global spatiotemporal scales; a framework of ego-centric ideas and beliefs that serves to guide decision making and action, and to generate, sustain, and apply knowledge.

concepts.name: deliberation
concepts.definition: the process of judging the merits of multiple options, which may then be followed by choice.

concepts.name: thought
concepts.definition: Subjectively salient cognitive processing, at least part of which may be reportable.

concepts.name: delusion
concepts.definition: A belief held despite appreciable external evidence to the contrary.

concepts.name: addiction
concepts.definition: A phenomenon sometimes conflated and sometimes contrasted with dependency, in which a person has transitioned from liking a rewarding substance or behavior to requiring it.

concepts.name: optical illusion
concepts.definition: A phenomenon in which what is visually perceived does not reflect the nature of the objective stimulus.

concepts.name: Gestalt grouping
concepts.definition: the ways in which elements are perceived to be grouped together, most often described for auditory and visual perception, but may also be a factor for other modalities

concepts.name: inattentional blindness
concepts.definition: a phenomenon in which people fail to see an unexpected stimulus

concepts.name: interoception
concepts.definition: perception of stimuli inside the body, e.g. hunger, thirst, pain

concepts.name: extinction
concepts.definition: the phenomenon by which a response to a conditional stimulus presented in absence of the unconditional stimulus diminishes over time; rather than a forgetting, it is generally believed to be a new learning.

concepts.name: difference threshold
concepts.definition: the smallest detectable difference between two stimuli

concepts.name: binocular depth cue
concepts.definition: a cue that provides depth information about a scene when it is viewed with both eyes

concepts.name: color constancy
concepts.definition: the ability to assign stable colors despite variation in light, i.e. identifying that a given box is orange irrespective of the spectral composition or intensity of the light illuminating it

concepts.name: feature search
concepts.definition: search for a target according to a single feature (e.g. color)

concepts.name: attentional blink
concepts.definition: a phenomenon in which the participant is unable to detect a second salient visual stimulus if presented at the same spatial location within 200-500 milliseconds after the first

concepts.name: change blindness
concepts.definition: the inability to detect changes to an object or a scene even if large, repeatedly made, or anticipated; it can even occur when the subject is fixated on the item being changed.

concepts.name: motion aftereffect
concepts.definition: the illusion of movement in a stationary object after prolonged viewing of a moving object

concepts.name: overt attention
concepts.definition: directing a sense organ at a stimulus source

concepts.name: covert attention
concepts.definition: the act of focusing on one of several sensory stimuli

concepts.name: unconscious perception
concepts.definition: the process of perceiving a stimulus without being conscious of having seen it, measurable by electrophysiological response at the time and by recognition testing later

concepts.name: autonoesis
concepts.definition: consciousness of self consistent over time, both in imagining the future and recalling the past; consciousness of subjectivity

concepts.name: visual awareness
concepts.definition: the subjective experience of seeing, emerging about 200ms after the onset of a visual stimulus; it is contrasted with unconscious visual perception

concepts.name: psychological refractory period
concepts.definition: the phenomenon by which people are unable to make more than one conscious decision (and, by extension, unable to complete more than one task) within a few hundred milliseconds

concepts.name: noesis
concepts.definition: a consciousness characterized by knowing or familiarity without self-reference (contrast with autonoesis)

concepts.name: Risk Taking
concepts.definition: accepting a challenging task that simultaneously involves potential for failure as well as for accomplishment or personal benefit. It is often associated with creativity and taking calculated risks in the workplace or in educational settings.

concepts.name: impulsivity
concepts.definition: the tendency to act without adequately assessing context

concepts.name: binocular rivalry
concepts.definition: competition between the eyes for control of perception, particularly evident when different stimuli are presented to each eye

concepts.name: cone of confusion
concepts.definition: a region around the head for which neither interaural time differences (ITDs) nor interaural loudness differences (ILDs) in a sound are not great enough for a person to localize the sound source

concepts.name: vection
concepts.definition: the illusion of movement in a stationary person caused by moving visual cues

concepts.name: visual acuity
concepts.definition: a measure of the finest resolution perceivable by the eyes

concepts.name: visual angle
concepts.definition: the angle a viewed object subtends at the eye, usually stated in degrees of arc, and is a function of the size of the object and its distance from the eye

concepts.name: domain specificity
concepts.definition: the idea in cognitive science that the mind is divided according to the content of information being processed into specialized, possibly evolved, modules

concepts.name: global precedence
concepts.definition: the idea that, all else held equal, global features are perceived earlier than are local features of a given stimulus

concepts.name: anxiety
concepts.definition: An aversive psychophysiological state characterized by fear, worry, or concern associated with current or impending threat often elicited by general and specific interoceptive or exteroceptive cues.

concepts.name: spontaneous recovery
concepts.definition: recovery of a conditioned response following extinction, simply as a function of time

concepts.name: reinstatement
concepts.definition: following extinction, conditioned response returns after exposure to unconditional stimulus (US) alone

concepts.name: blindsight
concepts.definition: unconscious visual perception, i.e. a phenomenon in which people can detect, discriminate between, and respond to visual stimuli without being consciously aware of them

concepts.name: feature integration
concepts.definition: how different features of a percept are bound into a conscious whole

concepts.name: transduction
concepts.definition: in which information from stimuli is transduced into signals to the brain

concepts.name: phototransduction
concepts.definition: in which energy from visual stimuli is transduced into a signal in the retina to the brain

concepts.name: border ownership
concepts.definition: the determination of a local feature (i.e. a contrast edge or line) and the object to which it belongs

concepts.name: multistable perception
concepts.definition: conflicting sensory input results in spontaneous, sometimes controllable, experiences thereof

concepts.name: visual orientation
concepts.definition: use of visual stimulus information in perceiving orientation thereof or of the self

concepts.name: lateral masking
concepts.definition: perceptual phenomenon in which one stimulus attenuates signals generated by another, adjacent, stimulus presented simultaneously

concepts.name: crowding
concepts.definition: target stimulus is made harder to identify when surrounded by similar non-target stimuli

concepts.name: lexeme
concepts.definition: the phonological form of a given lexical item being retrieved

concepts.name: trait anxiety
concepts.definition: a hyper-responsive system for threat detection, differentiated from state anxiety in duration and cause

concepts.name: strength
concepts.definition: Strength refers to a muscle's ability to generate force against physical objects.

concepts.name: balance
concepts.definition: Balance allows humans to be able to orient the body in space, maintain an upright posture under static and dynamic conditions, and move without falling, by adjusting motoric control

concepts.name: locomotion
concepts.definition: Locomotion is the act of moving the body from one place to another. It requires input from the brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, muscular power and joint and cardiovascular health.

concepts.name: vestibular control
concepts.definition: The vestibular system transduces and processes angular and linear acceleration and deceleration of the head, enabling postural balance, locomotor control, and gaze stabilization, particularly during head movement. The vestibular system is an integral component of our sensory experience and sensory-motor function. Healthy peripheral and central vestibular anatomy is essential for functionally relevant gaze stability during head motion and postural control.

concepts.name: life satisfaction
concepts.definition: Oneâs cognitive evaluation of life experiences; this measure is concerned with whether people like their lives or not. Life satisfaction includes both general (e.g., my life is going well) and domain-specific (e.g., I am satisfied with my family life) aspects.

concepts.name: attentional bias
concepts.definition: Attentional bias refers to the tendency for a particular class of stimuli to capture attention. The term is most typically used to refer to biases related to emotional content in bottom-up-capture attention tasks.

concepts.name: reception of facial communication
concepts.definition: The capacity to perceive someoneâs emotional state non-verbally based on facial expressions. Examples include affect recognition, facial recognition and characterization.

concepts.name: productive facial communication
concepts.definition: The capacity to convey oneâs emotional state non-verbally via facial expressions, including eye contact, expressive reciprocation, and gaze following.

concepts.name: Reception of non-facial communication
concepts.definition: The capacity to perceive social and emotional information based on modalities other than facial expression, including non-verbal gestures, affective prosody, distress calling, cooing, etc.

concepts.name: Production of non-facial communication
concepts.definition: The capacity to express social and emotional information based on modalities other than facial expression, including non-verbal gestures, affective prosody, distress calling, cooing, etc.

concepts.name: agency
concepts.definition: The ability to recognize oneâs self as the agent of oneâs actions and thoughts, including the recognition of oneâs own body/body parts.

concepts.name: self knowledge
concepts.definition: The ability to make judgments about oneâs current cognitive or emotional internal states, traits, and/or abilities.

concepts.name: animacy perception
concepts.definition: The ability to appropriately perceive that another entity is an agent (i.e., has a face, interacts contingently, and exhibits biological motion).

concepts.name: action perception
concepts.definition: The perception of an action being performed by an animate entity.

concepts.name: understanding mental states
concepts.definition: The ability to make judgments and/or attributions about the mental state of other animate entities that allows one to predict or interpret their behaviors. Mental state refers to intentions, beliefs, desires, and emotions.

concepts.name: circadian rhythm
concepts.definition: Endogenous, self-sustaining oscillations that organize the timing of biological systems to optimize physiology, behavior, and health. Circadian rhythms are synchronized by recurring environmental cues and attempt to anticipate the external environment. They also modulate homeostasis within the brain and other systems, tissues, and organs.

concepts.name: sleep
concepts.definition: Sleep and wakefulness are endogenous, recurring, behavioral states that reflect coordinated changes in the dynamic functional organization of the brain and that optimize physiology, behavior, and health. Homeostatic and circadian processes regulate the propensity for wakefulness and sleep. Sleep is a reversible state, characterized by postural recumbence, behavioral quiescence, and reduced responsiveness. It involves predictable cycling of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM). It is affected by experiences during wakefulness, and has restorative and transformative effects that optimize neurobehavioral functions during wakefulness.

concepts.name: loss
concepts.definition: A state of deprivation of a motivationally significant con-specific, object, or situation. Loss may be social or non-social and may include permanent or sustained loss of monetary values, shelter, behavioral control, status, loved ones, or relationships. The response to loss may be episodic (e.g., grief) or sustained.

concepts.name: defensive aggression
concepts.definition: A response elicited by a real or perceived threat that leads to a pattern of behaviors directed at terminating the threat.

concepts.name: offensive aggression
concepts.definition: A response elicited by competition over resource acquisition or other positive consequences. This form of aggression often arises from differences in social status and dominance.

concepts.name: reward valuation
concepts.definition: Processes by which the probability and benefits of a prospective outcome are computed and calibrated by reference to external information, social context (e.g., group input, counterfactual comparisons), and/or prior experience. This calibration is influenced by pre-existing biases, learning, memory, stimulus characteristics, and deprivation states. Reward valuation may involve the assignment of incentive salience to stimuli.

concepts.name: effort valuation
concepts.definition: Processes by which the cost(s) of obtaining an outcome is computed; tendency to overcome response costs to obtain a reinforcer.

concepts.name: reward learning
concepts.definition: A process by which organisms acquire information about stimuli, actions, and contexts that predict positive outcomes, and by which behavior is modified when a novel reward occurs or outcomes are better than expected. Reward learning is a type of reinforcement learning, and similar processes may be involved in learning related to negative reinforcement.

concepts.name: semantic network
concepts.definition: Set of concepts and relations

concepts.name: cognitive training
concepts.definition: Targeted exercises designed to help improve mental capacities.

concepts.name: emotion regulation
concepts.definition: The ability to have control over and change emotional responses, such as feelings and behaviors associated with them.

concepts.name: neuroplasticity
concepts.definition: The brain's ability to change in structure and function through experience.

concepts.name: restricted behavior
concepts.definition: A restricted behavior is a stereotyped pattern of behavior, activity, or interest. Examples include preoccupation with an object, activity, or topic, and this preoccupation is abnormal in intensity or focus.  Individuals with restricted behaviors may find it challenging to break away from habit or routine.

concepts.name: social motivation
concepts.definition: An individual's tendency to seek out direct contact with another person or a group of people.

concepts.name: irritability
concepts.alias: anger, agitation, moodiness, testy, grumpy, short tempered
concepts.definition: The quality or state of being agitated, testy, grumpy, moody, or having a short temper.

concepts.name: lethargy
concepts.definition: a lack of energy or enthusiasm.  In a social context, this means being socially withdrawn.

concepts.name: hyperactivity
concepts.definition: a condition characterized by excessive restlessness and movement, and commonly non-compliance

concepts.name: Inappropriate speech
concepts.definition: dialogue, either to oneself or others, that is not appropriate or suitable to the current situation

concepts.name: internalizing
concepts.definition: focusing negative energy on the self, often through holding back emotion, often leading to less than ideal emotional states (worry, anxiety, negativity and depression).  These states are frequently present in autistic children.

concepts.name: externalizing
concepts.definition: attributing cause to factors outside of the self

concepts.name: conduct disorder
concepts.definition: Lacking regard for others and callous, unemotional.  Characterized by repetitive and persistent pattern of behavior in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate norms are violated.

concepts.name: antisocial personality
concepts.definition: avoiding the company of other people, unsociable, sometimes to the extent of injuring others or the interests of society in general

concepts.name: defiance
concepts.definition: bold resistance to an opposing force, power, or authority, expressed through behavior and attitude

concepts.name: obsession
concepts.definition: compulsive preoccupation with a fixed idea or an unwanted feeling or emotion, often accompanied by symptoms of anxiety

concepts.name: social phobia
concepts.definition: having a fear so strong of being judged by others and of being embarrassed that it significantly gets in the way of everyday life

concepts.name: rigidity
concepts.definition: unable to stray from a particular pattern of behavior or thought

concepts.name: agreeableness
concepts.definition:
Agreeableness is a personality trait manifesting itself in individual behavioral characteristics that are perceived as kind, sympathetic, cooperative, warm and considerate.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agreeableness

concepts.name: openness
concepts.definition:
Openness to experience is one of the domains which are used to describe human personality in the Five Factor Model. Openness involves active imagination, aesthetic sensitivity, attentiveness to inner feelings, preference for variety, and intellectual curiosity.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Openness_to_experience

concepts.name: psychosis
concepts.definition: A kind of disordered thinking for which thought and emotions are so impaired that contact is lost with external reality.

concepts.name: paranoia
concepts.definition: a mental condition characterized by delusions of persecution, unwarranted jealousy, or exaggerated self-importance, typically elaborated into an organized system. It may be an aspect of chronic personality disorder, of drug abuse, or of a serious condition such as schizophrenia in which the person loses touch with reality.

concepts.name: phonological awareness
concepts.definition: Explicit awareness of the abstract units that compose spoken words, including syllables, onset and rime units, and individual phonemes.

concepts.name: guilt
concepts.definition: a cognitive or an emotional experience that occurs when a person realizes or believes (whether it is true or not) that he or she has compromised his or her own standards of conduct or has violated a moral standard, and bears significant responsibility for that violation.

concepts.name: anhedonia
concepts.definition: lack of interest

concepts.name: appetite
concepts.definition: the desire to eat food

concepts.name: fatigue
concepts.definition: a feeling of weariness, tiredness, or lack of energy

concepts.name: suicidal ideation
concepts.definition: thoughts about or an unusual preoccupation with suicide

concepts.name: perfectionism
concepts.definition: a personality trait characterized by a person's striving for flawlessness and setting excessively high performance standards, accompanied by overly critical self-evaluations and concerns regarding others' evaluations.

concepts.name: eating
concepts.definition: An individual's preferences for food or general appetite.

concepts.name: sensory defensiveness
concepts.definition: a condition defined as having "a tendency to react negatively or with alarm to sensory input which is generally considered harmless or non-irritating" to neurotypical people."

concepts.name: sensitivity to change
concepts.definition: an individual's ability to withstand changes in his or her environment or situation.

concepts.name: noise sensitivity
concepts.definition: having a tendency to react negatively or with alarm to noise input which is generally considered harmless or non-irritating to neurotypical individuals.

concepts.name: loneliness
concepts.definition:
loneliness is a complex and unpleasant emotional response to isolation or lack of companionship.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loneliness

concepts.name: phonological processing
concepts.definition: Refers to the use of phonological information (i.e., the sound of one's language) in processing written and oral language.

concepts.name: conflict adaptation effect
concepts.definition:
The congruency effect after incongruent trials is reduced when compared with congruent trials. It is a trial-to-trial effect. Originally reported by Gratton, Coles, and Donchin (1992; as refered by van Steenbergen, 2010; Psychological Science). Thus:
(iI-iC)

concepts.name: goal selection
concepts.definition: None

concepts.name: discrimination
concepts.definition: Responding differently to stimuli that differ in some aspect

concepts.name: stimulus detection
concepts.definition: It is the ability to discern between information-bearing patterns and random patterns that distract from the information

concepts.name: visual localization
concepts.definition: Localization of visually perceived objects relative to other visually perceived objects (either simultaneously or successively) or relative to a visual norm, or by absolute identification.

concepts.name: perceptual priming
concepts.definition: is based on the form of the stimulus and is enhanced by the match between the early and later stimuli.

concepts.name: spatial localization
concepts.definition: reference to a definite locality in space

concepts.name: Limited Capacity
concepts.definition: None

concepts.name: interference control
concepts.definition: Protection from self-directed responses that result from disruption by competing events and responses.

concepts.name: object-based attention
concepts.definition: refers to the relationship between an âobjectâ representation and a personâs visually stimulated, selective attention

concepts.name: conceptual priming
concepts.definition: Conceptual priming is based on the meaning of a stimulus and is enhanced by semantic tasks. For example, table, will show priming effects on chair, because table and chair belong to the same category.

concepts.name: positive priming
concepts.definition: refers to increased speed of processing of priming caused by simply experiencing the stimulus

concepts.name: repetition priming
concepts.definition: refers to the finding that an initial presentation of a stimulus influences the way in which an individual will respond to that stimulus when it is presented at a later time.

concepts.name: semantic priming
concepts.definition: is where we process stimuli better depending on what comes first.

concepts.name: associative priming
concepts.definition: In associative priming, the target is a word that has a high probability of appearing with the prime, and is "associated" with it but not necessarily related in semantic features.

concepts.name: response priming
concepts.definition: A special form of the visuomotor priming effect in which prime and target are presented in quick succession.

concepts.name: kindness priming
concepts.definition: is a specific form of priming that occurs when a subject experiences an act of kindness and subsequently experiences a lower threshold of activation when subsequently encountering positive stimuli.

concepts.name: negative priming
concepts.definition: is a kind of priming in which the speed of processing is slower than unprimed levels. It is caused by experiencing the stimulus and then ignoring it

concepts.name: feature-based attention
concepts.definition: direct limited processing resources on those sensory inputs that are most relevant for the task at hand

concepts.name: punishment processing
concepts.definition: the authoritative imposition of an undesirable or unpleasant outcome upon a group or individual, in response to a particular action or behaviour that is deemed unacceptable or threatening to some norm (from Wikipedia.org)

concepts.name: shape recognition
concepts.definition: the ability to perceive a shape

concepts.name: relational comparison
concepts.definition: Comparison of two stimuli based on a relational feature

concepts.name: animacy decision
concepts.definition: decision about whether a stimulus exhibits animacy

concepts.name: auditory tone detection
concepts.definition: determining the presence of an auditory stimulus such as a sound or tone

concepts.name: auditory tone discrimination
concepts.definition: It is the ability to perceive and respond to differences among auditory stimuli

concepts.name: body maintenance
concepts.definition: keeping information about the body in active and immediately accessible state.

concepts.definition: assigning a detected color stimulus into a category (not necessarily task defined)

concepts.name: decision certainty
concepts.definition: the confidence of knowledge regarding the likelihood of an outcome.

concepts.name: economic value processing
concepts.definition: the process of comparing, at an idiosyncratic level, the economic value of two or more options.

concepts.name: emotional face recognition
concepts.definition: The process of determining whether an emotional face is the same as another face that has been previously encountered.

concepts.name: potential monetary loss
concepts.definition: A potential negative return in the form of money for performance of a specific behavior.

concepts.name: potential monetary reward
concepts.definition: A potential positive return in the form of money for performance of a specific behavior.

concepts.name: proactive control
concepts.definition: Top down modulation of cognitive processes in anticipation of future goals or task demands. Often involves reaction time slowing

concepts.name: reinforcement learning

concepts.name: reward anticipation
concepts.definition: prior expectation of the occurrence of a reward, sometimes accompanied by an emotional reaction

concepts.name: risk processing
concepts.definition: the extraction of information about the potential or current risk associated with a stimulus

concepts.name: selective control
concepts.definition: Top-down modulation of specific response output or of specific stimuli in the environment.

concepts.name: semantic categorization
concepts.definition: The assignment of a semantic stimulus to one of a set of categories.

concepts.name: spatial selective attention
concepts.definition: The process of dedicating cognitive and perceptual resources to one or more spatial inputs and attenuating receptiveness to other inputs.

concepts.name: string maintenance
concepts.definition: The process of keeping string (e.g., consonant)  information in active and immediately accessible state.

concepts.name: task difficulty
concepts.definition: the perceived effort required to complete some mental or physical activity

concepts.name: tool maintenance

concepts.definition: visual detection of instances of objects of a certain class (such as humans, buildings, cars, etc.).

concepts.definition: The process of identifying a meaningful pattern in visual stimuli.

concepts.name: intertemporal choice
concepts.definition:
the study of how people make choices about what and how much to do at various points in time, when choices at one time influence the possibilities available at other points in time.

https://en.wikipedia.org/?title=Intertemporal_choice

concepts.definition: the process of comparing, at an idiosyncratic level, the relatively desirability of two or more options or the internal idiosyncratic value represented internally for such a judgement

concepts.definition: Subjective food value is used as term to indicate a food's worth, based on an individuals' current desires and needs (e.g., hunger). Subjective food value assessment is an intermediate  step during food decision making.

A behavioral phenomena for which a participant in an experiment is biased to respond in a particular way.

concepts.name: Dyslexia
concepts.definition: Dyslexia is a reading impairment. There are currently 17 known types of dyslexia, each resulting from a different component of the reading process, each with different error types and different characteristics. Dyslexia can result from brain damage after reading has been acquired (acquired dyslexia), or can be present from birth (developmental dyslexia).

concepts.name: Surface dyslexia
concepts.definition: surface dyslexia is a reading impairment, which can be acquired or developmental. It results from a deficit in the lexical route for word reading. As a result, the reader needs to rely on the sublexical for reading, reading by converting each letter or group of letters (grapheme) to a sound (phoneme). Surface dyslexia is characterised by slow reading (because reading via grapheme-to-phoneme conversion is slower than reading via the lexical route); it is also characterised by incorrect reading aloud of irregular words (such as talk, sure, none, and comb).

Transferring QuickBooks to a new computer can seem like a daunting task, but with the right guidance, it can be a smooth and hassle-free process. Whether you're upgrading your hardware or switching to a different computer, it's essential to ensure that your financial data remains intact and accessible. In this article, we will provide you with a step-by-step guide on how to transfer QuickBooks to a new computer.

Now, let's get into the step-by-step guide on how to transfer QuickBooks to a new computer:

Step 1: Install QuickBooks on the New Computer

Insert your QuickBooks installation CD or download the software from the official QuickBooks website.

Follow the on-screen instructions to install QuickBooks on your new computer. When prompted, enter your product key.

After installation, do not open QuickBooks yet.

Step 2: Copy Your QuickBooks Data Files

On your old computer, locate your QuickBooks company files. These files usually have extensions like .QBW or .QBB.

Copy these files to an external storage device, such as a USB drive, external hard drive, or cloud storage service.

Connect the external storage device to your new computer.

Paste the copied QuickBooks company files into a location on your new computer. The default location for these files is typically in the "Documents" or "Public Documents" folder.

Step 3: Restore Your Backup

Open QuickBooks on your new computer.

Go to the "File" menu and select "Open or Restore Company."

Choose "Restore a backup copy" and click "Next."

Follow the on-screen instructions to locate and select the backup file you copied to your new computer. This file will have a .QBB extension.

Complete the restoration process by following the prompts.

Step 4: Reactivate QuickBooks

When you open QuickBooks on your new computer, you may be prompted to activate the software. Use your product key and follow the activation process.

If you encounter any issues with activation, contact QuickBooks support for assistance.

Step 5: Verify Data and Settings

After transferring your data, take some time to verify that all your financial data, settings, and preferences have been successfully transferred to the new computer.

Test the software to ensure that everything is working as expected.

concepts.name: Pavlovian bias
concepts.definition:
Pavlovian bias (also called motivational bias) denotes that phenomenon that 
- reward-related cues (eliciting reward anticipation) invigorate action (lead to more active "Go" responses and speed up these Go responses)
- punishment-related cues (eliciting punishment anticipation) suppress action (lead to less "Go" / more "NoGo" responses and slow down Go responses).

This phenomenon is often believed to arise based on asymmetric nature of the direct ("Go") and indirect ("NoGo") pathway in the basal ganglia (Frank, 2005, Collins & Frank, 2014). The direct pathway is assumed to "gate" / release actions, while the indirect pathway is believed to suppress/inhibit actions. The direct pathway features more dopamine D1 receptors (activated by high dopamine levels as in positive prediction errors elicited by rewards), while the indirect pathway features more dopamine D2/D3 receptors (activated by low dopamine levels as in negative prediction errors elicited by punishments). Hence, rewards should make the direct pathway more sensitive to input and thus facilitate action release, while punishments should make the indirect pathway more  sensitive to input and thus facilitate action suppression.

Pavlovian biases are typically measured with the motivational go/nogo learning task.
fMRI studies featuring this task having typically not found BOLD signal from the striatum/ basal ganglia to reflect reward vs. punishment anticipation (as predicted by the above basal ganglia model), but instead to reflect the executed response (Go vs. NoGo) (Guitart-Masip et al., 2011; Guitart-Masip, Huys et al., 2012; Guitart-Masip, Chowdhury et al., 2012; Moutoussis et al., 2018; Algermissen et al., 2021). Instead, cue valence (Win vs. Avoid) has been found to be encoded in vmPFC BOLD (positively) and ACC BOLD (negatively).

Pavlovian bias in behavior could arise from a response bias (i.e. reward/ punishment prospects biasing response selection), but also from biased action-outcome learning: A learning bias such that learning of Go responses after reward feedback is enhanced, while unlearning of NoGo responses after punishment feedback is attenuated, will also give rise to motivational biases (Swart et al., 2017, 2018; de Boer et al., 2019).
Pavlovian bias has been suggested as a response strategy in face of little control over the environment (Csifcsák et al., 2019; Dorfman & Gershman, 2019; Gershman et al., 2021).
